Les commentateurs rappellent d'abord que Dieu est exalté au-dessus de toute imperfection et de ce qu'attribuent les associateurs. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn al-Jawzi, al-Baghawi et al-Qurtubi expliquent que l'interdiction vise la précipitation à réciter avec Gabriel par crainte d'oublier, comme le dit le verset: « Ne remue pas ta langue pour le hâter ». Il faut écouter et attendre la fin de la récitation, puis réciter à son tour. Mujahid et Qatada donnent une autre lecture : ne pas réciter ni dicter le Coran aux gens avant que son sens ne soit clarifié, ce que rapportent aussi al-Tabari, al-Baghawi et al-Shawkani. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi et al-Baydawi comprennent que l'on vise l'empressement à recevoir la révélation et la course à la réciter avec l'ange, et que la demande de science supplémentaire montre que le savoir est ce qu'il faut chercher à accroître. Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Qurtubi et al-Shawkani rapportent diverses causes de révélation, dont l'affaire de l'homme qui frappa son épouse ; al-Razi, al-Baydawi et Ibn Kathir jugent toutefois ce récit faible ou ne s'y fient pas. Les commentateurs s'accordent sur la recommandation de demander à Dieu un surcroît de savoir et sur l'utilité de la patience et de l'écoute attentive dans l'apprentissage.

Dieu rappelle qu'Il avait engagé Adam auparavant, en lui ordonnant de ne pas approcher l'arbre interdit ; mais Adam a oublié cet engagement et n'a trouvé en lui aucune fermeté. Les commentateurs voient dans ce passage un réconfort pour le Prophète ﷺ : l'oubli et la transgression de l'alliance sont anciens chez les descendants d'Adam, et leur père lui-même y est tombé. Sur le sens de « fa-nasiya », al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Mujahid et al-Hasan y voient un abandon de l'ordre divin, tandis que d'autres, comme Ibn Abbas dans une transmission, retiennent l'oubli au sens strict, ce qui est selon certains une excuse et selon d'autres une négligence. Ibn 'Atiyya estime que l'oubli par simple distraction ne peut pas être visé ici, puisque le coupable n'est pas châtié dans ce cas. Quant à « 'azman », la plupart l'entendent comme la patience (Qatada, Muqatil), la conservation de l'ordre (Ibn Abbas, Ibn Zayd, Ata') ou la résolution ferme (Abu Hayyan, al-Zamakhshari). Al-Zamakhshari précise qu'il s'agit d'une volonté assez forte pour décourager Satan. Des commentateurs, dont al-Nasafi, ont tiré de ce verset que Adam n'était pas l'un des messagers doués de constance, tandis que d'autres y voient une louange de sa patience, qui surpasse selon un hadith celle de toute sa descendance. Ibn Sa'di souligne que l'homme est appelé « insan » parce qu'il oublie, et que la repentance d'Adam est exemplaire. Al-Shinqiti rappelle que les savants divergent sur l'excuse due à l'oubli avant la révélation de la règle islamique, et que les Prophètes restent à l'abri des fautes liées à la transmission.

Ce verset rappelle l'ordre donné par Dieu aux anges de se prosterner devant Adam : tous obéirent, sauf Iblis qui refusa par orgueil. Pour la plupart des commentateurs, ce récit sert de rappel après la mention de l'oubli d'Adam, afin de montrer l'hostilité d'Iblis envers lui. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi et Ibn Kathir expliquent que Dieu met en garde Adam contre cet ennemi, pour qu'il ne le laisse pas les expulser du Paradis, ce qui le ferait souffrir. Ibn Atiyya, Ibn al-Jawzi et al-Zamakhshari relèvent que le verbe est au singulier parce qu'Adam est le responsable de la famille et celui qui travaille, ce qui fait de lui celui qui peine davantage. Selon al-Baghawi et Ibn Kathir, cette peine désigne le labeur de la terre, les semailles, la mouture et la cuisson du pain, et ils citent la tradition rapportée par Sa'id ibn Jubayr d'un taureau roux qu'Adam faisait labourer. Le Paradis est décrit comme un lieu sans faim, sans nudité, sans soif ni ardeur du soleil. Sur la nature d'Iblis, Ibn 'Abbas, al-Nasafi et al-Baydawi affirment qu'il était un djinn qui adorait Dieu avec les anges, tandis qu'al-Hasan distingue la nature des anges de celle du feu d'Iblis. D'autres estiment qu'il faisait partie des anges, et l'exception serait alors continue. Quant au verbe « abā », al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi et Abu Hayyan y voient une phrase nouvelle qui indique que le refus venait de l'orgueil, son complément étant sous-entendu ou traité comme intransitif. Ibn Kathir rapporte aussi le hadith où Moïse dispute avec Adam, cité dans les recueils authentiques.

Les commentateurs expliquent que, après le refus d'Iblis de se prosterner devant Adam, Dieu avertit Adam que ce démon est un ennemi pour lui et pour son épouse. Il leur ordonne de ne pas lui obéir, car cela causerait leur expulsion du Jardin et Adam connaîtrait alors la peine. La plupart des exégètes entendent par « la peine » la fatigue de la subsistance : labourer, moissonner, moudre et cuire le pain. Le Jardin, en revanche, est un lieu où l'on n'a ni faim, ni nudité, ni soif, ni ardeur du soleil.

Al-Tabari et Ibn Kathir rapportent le récit transmis par Sa'id ibn Jubayr, selon lequel un taureau roux fut envoyé à Adam pour labourer, et qu'il essuyait la sueur de son front. Al-Sam'ani et al-Baghawi reprennent cette tradition, tandis qu'Ibn al-Jawzi et al-Qurtubi la mentionnent aussi. Le Qurtubi ajoute un autre récit selon lequel Adam eut à poursuivre un pain tombé de sa main. Al-Mawardi, Ibn al-Jawzi et al-Razi notent que la forme féminine n'est pas employée, car la peine revient surtout à l'homme, qui gagne le pain ; Al-Zamakhshari rappelle que le malheur de l'homme englobe celui de sa famille.

Le verbe « tomber dans la peine » est pris par Ibn Kathir et Ibn 'Ashur au sens de la fatigue quotidienne. Al-Razi, de son côté, relie ce passage à la suite de l'histoire, en rappelant qu'Adam avait oublié le pacte. Les lectures varient sur les versets suivants, ce qui est rappelé par Abu Hayyan et al-Shawkani. Al-Alusi souligne que l'expression « ennemi pour toi et ton épouse » répète la préposition pour insister sur l'hostilité, tandis qu'Ibn Sa'di insiste sur la plénitude des biens du Jardin. Les écrivains modernes, comme Sayyid Qutb et al-Sha'rawi, mettent l'accent sur la responsabilité de l'homme dans la subsistance du foyer.

Les commentateurs expliquent que ce verset énumère les bienfaits accordés à Adam au Paradis : ne pas avoir faim ni être nu, ne pas avoir soif ni subir la chaleur du soleil de midi, et cela aussi longtemps qu'il y demeure. La faim et la nudité font pendant à la soif et à l'ardeur du dhuha. Ibn al-Qayyim y voit une opposition précise : la faim est la douleur intérieure, la nudité la douleur extérieure, la soif la chaleur intérieure et le dhuha la chaleur extérieure, de sorte que le verset écarte toutes les souffrances. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi et Ibn Kathir expliquent que le dhuha désigne l'exposition au soleil, et Ikrima précise qu'il n'y a pas de soleil au Paradis, ses habitants étant à l'ombre étendue. Les grands commentateurs s'accordent à dire que ces quatre biens sont les piliers de la subsistance humaine, obtenus au Paradis sans effort ni travail. Al-Zamakhshari et al-Alusi voient dans cette suite de notions une rupture de correspondance destinée à énumérer les grâces séparément. Sur la lecture, Nafi' et Abu Bakr d'après 'Asim lisent « wa inna » avec kasra, tandis que les autres lisent avec fatha, et al-Tabari préfère cette dernière. Les commentateurs rattachent ensuite la mise en garde contre la fatigue terrestre : al-Razi, al-Qurtubi et Ibn 'Ashur y voient une allusion aux peines du travail sur terre, Sa'id ibn Jubayr évoquant le taureau roux qui labourait pour Adam. Le discours est adressé à Adam seul, car c'est lui qui assume le labeur.

Les commentateurs expliquent que Dieu annonce à Adam que, dans le Paradis, il ne connaîtra ni la faim ni la nudité, ni la soif ni l'ardeur du soleil, c'est-à-dire qu'il y disposera de sa subsistance, de ses vêtements et de son abri sans peine ni effort. Ibn 'Abbas et la plupart des exégètes, dont al-Tabari, entendent « ne pas être exposé au soleil » au sens propre, tandis que Ibn Kathir et al-Baghawi rappellent qu'il n'y a pas de soleil au Paradis et que ses habitants vivent sous une ombre étendue. Ce passage est généralement rattaché à la mise en garde contre Satan : sortir du Paradis entraînerait la fatigue du travail de la terre. Sur le plan de la lecture, tous s'accordent sur le fait que « wa anna-ka » avec fatha est une coordination à « allā tajū' », tandis que Nafi' et Abu Bakr lisent avec kasra, en reprise ou en coordination avec « inna laka ». Al-Tabari retient la fatha comme plus juste. Al-Zamakhshari et Ibn al-Qayyim relèvent la beauté de l'agencement, qui associe la faim à la nudité et la soif à l'ardeur du soleil, selon une correspondance entre douleur intérieure et extérieure, et qui énumère chaque bienfait séparément. Les commentateurs s'accordent sur le fait que ces versets décrivent l'état du Paradis avant la désobéissance, sans trancher entre les divergences sur les détails de la tentation et la nature de l'arbre.

Ce verset rapporte que le Diable chuchota à Adam, lui proposant de le guider vers l'arbre de l'éternité et une royauté impérissable. Les commentateurs s'accordent sur le sens de la waswasa, une suggestion secrète et séduisante, et sur le fait que le Diable attribua l'arbre à l'éternité parce que celui qui en mange, selon la croyance, ne meurt pas. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir et al-Baghawi rapportent, d'après Ibn 'Abbas, al-Sudi et Qatada, que l'arbre donnait une vie sans fin et un pouvoir qui ne s'éteint pas, promesse qui était mensongère. Al-Razi, al-Qadi et Ibn 'Atiyya considèrent que la suggestion fut un échange verbal audible, alors que d'autres pensent qu'elle fut une idée insinuée dans l'âme ; al-Qurtubi penche pour l'échange direct, en se fondant sur la lettre du texte. Les exégètes s'accordent aussi sur le fait que l'arbre précis n'est pas connu avec certitude, de sorte que son identification n'apporte pas grand-chose. Le sens du mot yabla fait débat : certains le traduisent par « ne périt pas », d'autres par « ne s'use pas » ou « ne cesse pas ». Selon la majorité, cette promesse fut le motif qui poussa Adam à manger de l'arbre interdit ; al-Zamakhshari et al-Nasafi insistent sur la séduction par la promesse d'immortalité et de pouvoir. Ibn 'Ashur explique que la question d'al-Diable est une proposition, et que le Diable n'indiqua pas l'arbre interdit mais un autre, ce qui fit croire à Adam qu'il y trouverait l'éternité. Les commentaires retiennent ainsi que le verset met en garde contre la séduction par le désir de longue vie et de pouvoir.

Ce verset rapporte qu'Adam et Ève mangèrent de l'arbre interdit, et que leurs parties intimes leur apparurent alors qu'elles leur étaient cachées auparavant. Ils se mirent à coller des feuilles du Paradis sur eux pour se couvrir, et Adam désobéit à son Seigneur et s'égara. Selon la plupart des commentateurs, dont al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi et al-Baydawi, c'est Satan qui les a incités à manger en promettant l'immortalité et une royauté éternelle. Le verbe « égarer » est entendu par la plupart comme une perte du but recherché, l'immortalité, ou comme un écart par rapport au droit chemin. Ibn Qutayba affirme qu'on peut dire qu'Adam a désobéi, mais non qu'il était « désobéissant », de même qu'on dit d'un homme qui a cousu un vêtement qu'il a cousu, sans en faire un tailleur. Al-Razi, al-Qurtubi et al-Alusi rapportent les réponses des savants à la question de la faute des prophètes : certains la situent avant la prophétie, d'autres la comprennent comme une petite faute ou une omission de ce qui était préférable. Al-Zamakhshari, en revanche, insiste sur la portée de réprimande du terme employé, et rejette l'interprétation qui ferait de « égarer » le sens de s'être gavé de nourriture. Concernant les feuilles, Mujahid et Qatada disent qu'elles étaient recousues comme un vêtement, tandis qu'Ibn Abbas et Ibn Jubayr parlent de feuilles de figuier. Le verset se conclut sur le fait que Dieu l'a élu après sa faute, lui a accordé le repentir et l'a guidé, ce que les commentateurs entendent comme une élection et une aide à la repentance.

Ce passage indique qu'après la désobéissance et l'égarement d'Adam, Dieu l'a élu et rapproché de Lui, a accepté son repentir et l'a guidé à y persévérer. Les commentateurs s'accordent à dire que l'élection (ijtiba') signifie le choix et la proximité, que le repentir (tawba) est l'agrément divin au retour d'Adam, et que la guidance (hudan) est le soutien qui lui permet de rester dans le repentir et de garder les moyens de la préservation. Al-Tabari précise que l'élection suit la désobéissance et qu'elle lui accorda de revenir à ce qui plaît à Dieu. Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Baydawi et al-Alusi rappellent que la racine du mot évoque la réunion et le choix. Al-Shinqiti relie le repentir aux paroles qu'Adam reçut de son Seigneur, selon le verset de la Vache.

La nature de la faute divise les avis. Al-Razi et Ibn Fûrak estiment qu'elle eut lieu avant la prophétie, tandis qu'al-Qurtubi rapporte qu'elle peut être considérée comme une petite faute ou un manquement à ce qui est préférable, et qu'Ibn 'Ashur juge qu'Adam n'était pas encore prophète et que ce passage n'autorise ni ne prohibe la faute chez les prophètes. Ibn Kathir et al-Qurtubi citent le hadith du débat entre Adam et Moïse, où Adam l'emporte parce que Dieu avait décrété la faute avant sa création. Al-Sha'rawi, lui, n'entre pas dans ce débat et voit dans l'élection le début de la prophétie.

Les commentateurs expliquent que ce verset s'adresse à Adam et Ève, et selon certains il inclut aussi Iblis avec eux ; pour d'autres, il s'adresse à Adam et à sa descendance ainsi qu'à Iblis et la sienne. Il s'agit de la descente du Paradis vers la terre, et l'inimitié entre les deux parties demeure : al-Zamakhshari et al-Nasafi la comprennent comme une rivalité dans la vie matérielle, et al-Nasafi y voit aussi une opposition religieuse. Tous s'accordent à dire que la guidance mentionnée est la clarification venue de Dieu par les Livres et les messagers, et que celui qui la suit ne s'égare pas en ce monde et ne sera pas malheureux dans l'au-delà. Ibn 'Abbas rapporte que Dieu a garanti cela à celui qui récite le Coran et y conforme sa conduite, avis appuyé par al-Sha'bi et plusieurs autres. Al-Zamakhshari et Ibn 'Atiyya expliquent le malheur comme le châtiment de l'égarement dans l'au-delà, de sorte que l'absence de malheur découle de l'absence d'égarement. Al-Razi estime que la guidance englobe les preuves et leur mise en pratique, et que la négation est générale, dans ce monde comme dans l'autre.

Quant à celui qui se détourne du rappel, il aura une vie étroite. Sur le sens de cette vie étroite, les avis divergent largement. Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ikrima et al-Dahhak y voient un gain illicite ou une subsistance impure ; al-Hasan, Qatada et Ibn Zayd y voient le zaqqum et le dari' en enfer ; Ibn Mas'ud, Abu Sa'id al-Khudri et Abu Hurayra, suivis par al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir et al-Razi, y voient le châtiment de la tombe et son étreinte. Ibn 'Atiyya et al-Razi rapportent d'autres explications, comme l'angoisse et l'étroitesse de la vie ici-bas. Le rassemblement aveugle est compris par Ibn 'Abbas et al-Zamakhshari comme une cécité physique, et par Mujahid comme une cécité à l'égard de la preuve.

Le verset établit ainsi clairement que suivre la guidance mène à la sécurité, tandis que s'en détourner conduit à l'étroitesse et à la cécité.

Les commentateurs expliquent que se détourner du rappel de Dieu désigne le fait de se détourner du Coran et de la guidance apportée par les messagers, c'est-à-dire de ne pas y croire et de ne pas agir selon ses prescriptions. Celui qui agit ainsi aura une vie étroite et pénible, sans sérénité ni apaisement du cœur, même si ses biens sont abondants. Il sera ressuscité aveugle le Jour de la résurrection. Les avis divergent sur la nature de cette cécité : Ibn 'Abbas et Mujahid y voient une cécité quant à l'argument, c'est-à-dire l'incapacité à trouver la preuve, tandis que d'autres y voient une cécité physique, position retenue par al-Tabari, Ibn al-Qayyim et Ibn Kathir qui concilient les deux états selon les moments. Quant à la vie étroite, de nombreux anciens l'ont rapportée au châtiment de la tombe, comme Abu Sa'id al-Khudri et Ibn Mas'ud, et al-Tabari retient cette lecture comme la plus juste en s'appuyant sur ce qui suit dans le verset. D'autres l'entendent comme une gêne ici-bas, née de la cupidité, de l'avarice et de la mauvaise opinion envers Dieu, ou comme une subsistance illicite selon 'Ikrima et al-Dahhak, ou encore comme le châtiment de la Géhenne avec le daria et le zaqqum selon al-Hasan et Qatada. Certains rassemblent ces sens et estiment que la vie étroite touche l'ici-bas, l'intermédiaire et l'au-delà. Al-Zamakhshari et d'autres commentent l'opposé : la foi apporte la sérénité même dans l'épreuve. Ibn Kathir précise que l'oubli du Coran après l'avoir mémorisé relève d'un autre avertissement.

Les commentateurs expliquent que celui qui se détourne du rappel de Dieu, c'est-à-dire de Son Livre et de Sa guidance, aura dans cette vie une existence étroite qui l'oppresse, même si ses moyens sont larges, et qu'il sera ressuscité aveugle le jour de la résurrection. Il demandera alors à son Seigneur, étonné : pourquoi m'as-tu ressuscité aveugle alors que je voyais ? Dieu lui répondra que Ses signes lui sont parvenus et qu'il les a oubliés, et que, de même, il sera aujourd'hui oublié dans le châtiment. Les exégètes s'accordent sur le fait que la rétribution est de même nature que l'acte. Pour le sens de la dureté de l'existence, la plupart expliquent le terme daank par l'étroitesse et la gêne ; Ibn 'Abbas et Mujahid y voient la misère ou une vie resserrée, tandis que 'Ikrima et al-Dahhak parlent de gain illicite ou de subsistance impure. Quant à l'existence étroite elle-même, Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, Abu Hurayra et Ibn Mas'ud y voient le châtiment de la tombe, al-Hasan et Qatada la nourriture de zaqqum et de darii en enfer, et d'autres un resserrement de la condition terrestre pour qui a mécru et mal pensé de Dieu. Sur la cécité, Mujahid l'entend comme aveuglement quant à l'argument, d'autres comme cécité de la vue ; Ibn 'Abbas rapporte que le ressuscité sort voyant puis devient aveugle en étant conduit vers le lieu du rassemblement. Al-Tabari comprend « j'étais clairvoyant » comme voyant par la preuve ou par les choses dans la vie d'ici-bas, et note que celui qui interroge ignore la faute qui lui vaut ce sort. Les lectures varient sur la voyelle de « a'mâ » et sur l'imala de l'alif.

Les commentateurs expliquent que ce verset est la réponse de Dieu à celui qui s'est détourné de Son rappel : ressuscité aveugle, il demande pourquoi on l'a rassemblé aveugle alors qu'il voyait. Il lui est répondu que, de même que Nos signes lui étaient venus et qu'il les a oubliés, il est aujourd'hui délaissé. Le châtiment est donc de même nature que la faute. La plupart, comme al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Nasafi et al-Jalalayn, s'accordent à dire que l'oubli signifie ici l'abandon et l'indifférence, et non la distraction, et qu'il sera laissé dans le Feu. Qatada précise qu'ils ont oublié le bien mais non le châtiment. Ibn Juzayy et Ibn Ashur y voient une métaphore de la privation de la miséricorde. Le verset précédent, sur la vie misérable (ma'isha dankan), a suscité des lectures divergentes : Ibn Abbas, Mujahid et al-Dahhak y voient la gêne ici-bas ou un gain illicite, al-Hasan et Qatada le Dari'e et le Zaqqum, tandis qu'Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, Ibn Mas'ud et Abu Hurayra y voient le châtiment de la tombe, opinion qu'al-Tabari retient. Quant à la cécité, Mujahid la comprend comme l'aveuglement quant à l'argument, d'autres comme cécité du regard, et al-Tabari la tient pour générale. Les commentateurs ne tranchent pas entre ces avis au-delà de leurs propres choix.

Les commentateurs expliquent que ce verset annonce à celui qui commet des excès et ne croit pas aux signes de son Seigneur un châtiment semblable à celui déjà décrit, et que le tourment de l'au-delà est plus terrible et plus durable. La plupart s'accordent à entendre par « l'excès » l'associationnisme ou la transgression généralisée des interdits, et voient dans l'absence de foi aux signes une explication de cet excès. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir et al-Qurtubi voient dans l'expression « plus durable » la permanence éternelle du châtiment de l'au-delà, qui ne prend jamais fin, tandis que la souffrance d'ici-bas s'achève.

Les avis divergent sur la « vie resserrée » mentionnée juste avant. Ibn Mas'ud, Abu Sa'id al-Khudri et al-Suddi y voient le châtiment de la tombe, al-Hasan et Qatada le Zaqqum et les épines de la Géhenne, tandis qu'Ibn 'Abbas et 'Ata' y voient l'angoisse qui habite l'incroyant même dans l'aisance matérielle. D'autres y voient un gain illicite ou des biens dont on ne craint pas Dieu. Al-Razi rapporte ces opinions et note qu'elles peuvent toutes se combiner.

Sur le sens de la cécité au Jour de la résurrection, Ibn 'Abbas et 'Ikrima parlent d'une cécité de la vue, Mujahid d'une cécité à l'égard de la preuve, et al-Jubba'i d'une incapacité à trouver le bon chemin. Al-Zamakhshari et Ibn 'Ashur considèrent que la comparaison entre la vie d'ici-bas et l'au-delà souligne le caractère permanent du tourment final.

Ce verset reproche aux associateurs leur indifférence à l'égard du sort des peuples que Dieu a fait périr avant eux. Ils passent dans les demeures de ces générations lors de leurs voyages et voient les traces de leur destruction, et ces traces sont une leçon pour ceux qui ont de la raison. Tabari, Ibn Kathir et Baghawi rapportent que les destinataires sont les Quraych, qui faisaient du commerce vers le Cham et passaient près des demeures de 'Ad, de Thamud et des cités de Loth. Tabari retient cette interprétation comme la plus juste, tout en reconnaissant qu'une autre lecture est possible. Ibn Kathir, lui, élargit le sens à l'ensemble des peuples qui ont rejeté les messagers et appelle à réfléchir sur leurs vestiges. Les commentateurs divergent sur le sujet du verbe « yahdi » : al-Kisa'i et les Kufiens y voient la proposition elle-même ou le mot « kam », tandis que Zamakhshari, Baydawi et Nasafi l'attribuent à Dieu, appuyés par la lecture « nahdi » à la première personne du pluriel. D'autres sous-entendent le sujet « la guidance » ou « la réflexion ». Pour le sens de « al-nuha », Tabari dit qu'il s'agit de la raison, Qatada des gens de piété, et Razi observe que ce terme désigne la raison qui retient des vices. Quant à la phrase suivante, la plupart des commentateurs entendent par « parole antérieure » le report du châtiment jusqu'au Jour dernier ou au jour de Badr, et par « terme fixé » le temps marqué pour leur châtiment, Ibn Kathir précisant que Dieu ne châtie personne sans qu'il ait reçu la preuve.

Les commentateurs expliquent que ce verset signifie que le châtiment qui a frappé les peuples anciens n'a pas frappé les Mecquois parce qu'une parole antérieure de Dieu a différé leur punition. Selon Ibn Kathir, al-Baydawi et Ibn 'Ashur, cette parole est la promesse de reporter le châtiment de cette communauté jusqu'à l'au-delà, tandis que al-Zamakhshari et al-Qasimi la comprennent de la même manière, comme une promesse de rétribution différée. Al-Tabari et Ibn Kathir voient dans le terme inexorable (lizam) la mort ou le châtiment, Ibn 'Abbas parlant de mort et Ibn Zayd de mise à mort. Quant au terme fixé, al-Tabari et Ibn Kathir le rapportent à la vie d'ici-bas ou à l'Heure, Ibn 'Atiyya et Ibn al-Jawzi l'expliquent aussi par le jour de Badr, rapporté dans al-Bukhari, et Qatada le rattache au Jour de la Résurrection. Al-Razi retient que la parole est un décret divin aux anges, et que la sagesse de ce report est cachée à Dieu selon les gens de la Sunna. Pour l'ordre de patience et de glorification, la plupart des exégètes, dont al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir et Ibn al-Jawzi, y voient les cinq prières : l'aube, l'asr, le maghrib et le isha, et la prière de midi. Al-Razi et al-Baydawi proposent d'autres répartitions. Concernant la lecture de « tarda », al-Tabari juge les deux lectures équivalentes, l'une signifiant que tu seras agréé par la récompense, l'autre que Dieu te satisfera.

Dieu ordonne à son Prophète ﷺ de supporter patiemment les propos de ses détracteurs, qui l'accusent de magie, de poésie ou de folie, et de glorifier son Seigneur en le louant à des moments précis. La plupart des commentateurs y voient les cinq prières : la prière de l'aube avant le lever du soleil, celle de l'après-midi avant son coucher, une partie des heures de la nuit pour le maghrib et le 'isha', et la prière de midi, située aux deux extrémités de la journée. Le but est d'obtenir le contentement que procure la récompense divine. Les exégètes s'accordent sur l'inversion de l'ordre des mots : c'est la parole antérieure de Dieu et le terme fixé qui retardent le châtiment, sans quoi celui-ci les aurait frappés sans délai. Quant au sens de « lizam », al-Tabari cite Ibn 'Abbas et Ibn Zayd, qui y voient la mort ou la mise à mort, tandis que Qatada situe le terme fixé au Jour de la Résurrection et d'autres à la bataille de Badr. Concernant « turda », la lecture majoritaire avec un fatha signifie que le Prophète sera agréé par la récompense, alors que celle de 'Asim et al-Kisa'i avec un damma signifie que son Seigneur le contentera ; al-Tabari juge les deux lectures équivalentes. Selon al-Kalbi et Muqatil, le verset serait abrogé par le verset du combat, mais d'autres estiment qu'il reste en vigueur. Les avis divergent aussi sur les « extrémités du jour » : il s'agit pour certains de midi seul, pour d'autres de l'aube et du maghrib, ou de l'aube, midi et l'après-midi. Le pluriel s'explique par la clarté de la dualité. Pour al-Razi et d'autres, glorifier Dieu signifie prier en Le louant, tandis qu'Abu Muslim et al-Razi lui-même préfèrent y voir la pureté de Dieu de toute imperfection.

Dieu ordonne à Son Prophète de ne pas fixer longuement son regard sur les biens dont Il a doté certains incroyants, car ce ne sont que l'éclat éphémère de la vie d'ici-bas, par lequel Il les met à l'épreuve, tandis que la subsistance de ton Seigneur est meilleure et plus durable. Les commentateurs s'accordent pour dire que les « épouses » désignent des catégories ou des semblables parmi les mécréants, que la « fleur » est l'ornement et l'éclat, et que le but de ces biens est l'épreuve. Al-Zamakhshari et al-Nasafi estiment que le simple regard n'est pas blâmable, et que l'interdit vise l'admiration et le désir, tandis qu'al-Qasimi et Ibn 'Ashur entendent par « allonger le regard » le fait de le prolonger. Les avis divergent sur le sens du mot « subsistance » : al-Baghawi et al-Tabari y voient la récompense de l'au-delà, al-Mawardi et Abu Hayyan la contentement, al-Zamakhshari le licite, et al-Razi et Ibn 'Atiyya ce que Dieu accorde aux croyants en conquêtes et butins. Le récit d'un prêt demandé par le Prophète à un juif, gagé sur une cuirasse, est rapporté par al-Tabari, al-Baghawi et d'autres, mais Ibn 'Atiyya, Ibn Kathir et al-Qurtubi le jugent problématique, la sourate étant mecquoise. Plusieurs commentateurs, dont Ibn Kathir et al-Qurtubi, en tirent qu'il faut inciter sa famille à la prière et se confier à Dieu pour la subsistance, car la fin heureuse appartient aux pieux.

Dieu ordonne à Son Prophète ﷺ d'enjoindre à sa famille la prière et de persévérer lui-même dans son accomplissement. Il lui précise qu'Il ne lui demande aucune subsistance, ni pour lui ni pour autrui, car c'est Lui qui pourvoit à ses besoins, et que la bonne issue appartient à ceux qui craignent Dieu. Les commentateurs entendent par « la famille » soit les proches du Prophète, soit son peuple, et certains y incluent tous ceux qui le suivent parmi sa communauté, comme al-Mawardi, Ibn al-Jawzi, al-Baghawi et al-Baydawi. Ils s'accordent pour donner au mot « patience » le sens de la persévérance dans la prière, et pour affirmer que Dieu se charge de la subsistance du Prophète et des siens afin qu'il se consacre à l'au-delà. Ibn Kathir rapporte que la subsistance vient à qui accomplit la prière d'une manière qu'il n'attendait pas. Plusieurs ont relevé que la prière est un recours lors des difficultés, et ils ont cité des traditions attribuées à 'Urwa ibn al-Zubayr, Bakr al-Muzani et 'Umar ibn al-Khattab. Al-Razi et Ibn 'Atiyya estiment que le verset invite le croyant à instruire les siens et à les aider à l'adoration. Sur le sens de « la bonne issue », Ibn 'Abbas et Mujahid y voient le salut des croyants qui ont suivi le Prophète, tandis que d'autres y voient le Paradis ou une fin heureuse ici-bas et dans l'au-delà. Al-Razi et al-Nasafi précisent que le verset n'autorise pas à délaisser le travail, mais demande de libérer le cœur pour l'adoration. Ibn 'Ashur explique que la négation de la demande de subsistance abolit les redevances que les gens avaient coutume de verser aux chefs, et que l'adoration est elle-même une forme de reconnaissance envers Dieu.

Ce verset rapporte la demande des polythéistes de La Mecque : pourquoi Muhammad ne nous apporte-t-il pas un signe de son Seigneur, comme les prophètes précédents, telle la chamelle de Salih ou la guérison de l'aveugle-né et du lépreux par Jésus ? Dieu leur répond que le signe le plus grand leur est déjà parvenu : le Coran, qui est l'évidence de ce qui se trouve dans les anciens feuillets, c'est-à-dire les récits des peuples passés. La plupart des commentateurs considèrent le Coran comme le plus grand des miracles, car le miracle est un fait extraordinaire attaché à celui qui prétend être prophète ; or il est venu par un homme illettré qui n'a fréquenté ni étudié auprès des gens du Livre. Al-Tabari, Mujahid, Qatada, Ibn al-Jawzi et Ibn Kathir rapportent que ces feuillets désignent la Torah et l'Évangile et leur annonce du prophète. Plusieurs, comme al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi, Abu al-Su'ud et al-Alusi, estiment que le Coran est lui-même la preuve, car les Écritures antérieures ont besoin de son témoignage pour être établies. Ibn Kathir et al-Tabari évoquent aussi l'idée que l'destruction des peuples qui ont exigé des signes puis ont nié doit servir d'avertissement. Les lecteurs diffèrent entre la lecture « ta'tihim » au féminin et « ya'tihim » au masculin. Le verset se conclut par une menace : chacun attend, et l'on saura qui suit la voie droite et qui est bien guidé.

Ce verset dit que si Dieu avait fait périr ces incrédules par un châtiment avant d'envoyer le Prophète et de révéler le Coran, ils auraient dit le Jour de la Résurrection : « Seigneur, pourquoi ne nous as-tu pas envoyé un messager, afin que nous suivions tes signes avant d'être humiliés et couverts de honte ? » Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir et al-Jalalayn y voient une parole qu'ils prononceront dans l'au-delà. Selon certains, le pronom « de avant lui » renvoie au Prophète, selon d'autres à la preuve claire ou au Coran. Ibn Kathir rappelle que le Coran est lui-même le plus grand des signes accordés au Prophète, de sorte qu'aucune excuse ne subsiste après sa révélation. Ibn 'Atiyya et Ibn 'Ashur estiment que le verset établit l'argument contre eux, puisque le messager est venu.

Al-Razi, Ibn 'Atiyya et al-Tabari rapportent le hadith d'Abu Sa'id sur les trois qui plaideront le Jour de la Résurrection : celui qui est mort pendant la période de vacance, le faible d'esprit et l'enfant. Ibn 'Atiyya juge que les Quraych ne relèvent pas de cette période, car ils avaient entendu parler de prophétie, tandis qu'al-Qadi met en doute la solidité du récit. Quant au mot « humiliation » (dhull) et « honte » (khizy), al-Baydawi et al-Qurtubi y voient, selon Ibn 'Abbas, un châtiment d'ici-bas pour le premier et l'Enfer pour le second, tandis qu'al-Jalalayn les place tous deux dans l'au-delà. Certains lecteurs ont lu les deux verbes au passif.

Dans la suite, « Dis : chacun attend » est expliqué par al-Tabari et Ibn Kathir comme une attente mutuelle de l'issue, et al-Mawardi propose que l'on attende la victoire ou la manifestation de la vérité. Al-Razi envisage une attente de la mort, de la récompense ou du châtiment après la mort, et précise que l'interrogation de « vous saurez » sert de menace et non de doute.

Dieu ordonne à Son Prophète ﷺ de dire aux polythéistes : chacun de nous et de vous attend l'issue de cette affaire. Attendez donc, car vous saurez bientôt qui sont les gens de la voie droite, c'est-à-dire le chemin rectiligne sans aucune déviation, et qui a été guidé. Les commentateurs s'accordent à voir dans ce verset une menace qui clôt le passage. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi et Ibn Kathir expliquent que les polythéistes disaient attendre que les aléas du temps emportent le Prophète, à sa mort ils seraient délivrés de lui ; la réponse est que les croyants aussi attendent, mais l'attente des croyants porte sur la victoire et la manifestation de la vérité. Ces auteurs précisent que la voie droite désigne la religion droite ou le chemin rectiligne. Al-Mawardi propose deux lectures : savoir par la victoire en ce monde qui est dans le vrai religion, ou savoir au Jour de la Résurrection qui mène au Paradis. Al-Qurtubi relève que le verset vise à la fois les incroyants qui attendent et les croyants qui attendent la victoire. Sur la grammaire, al-Farra' admettait que « qui » puisse être à l'accusatif, mais al-Zajjaj et la plupart des grammairiens le rejettent et en font un interrogatif au nominatif. Plusieurs lectures existent (« as-sawa' », « as-su'a », « as-suwayy »), que Zamakhshari et Abu Hayyan rattachent au sens de juste milieu, de bonté ou de mal, et qui rendent l'opposition entre égarement et direction. Ibn 'Ashur y voit une allusion à la supériorité des croyants, et note que la fin de la sourate répond à son début.
en: The surah opens with the disjointed letters Ta and Ha, and the commentators differ on their meaning. Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Ikrima, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, al-Hasan, Qatada and al-Dahhak report that the word means 'O man' in other languages, such as Nabataean, Syriac or Ethiopic. Al-Tabari supports this view with Arabic verses in which the tribe of 'Akk uses the word in this sense, and he reads the verse as meaning that the Qur'an was not sent down to make the Prophet suffer. Mujahid links this to the long night prayers that wore him out, and Ibn Kathir transmits the same report. Others, such as al-Mahdawi, al-Razi, Abu Hayyan and Ibn 'Atiyya, consider it more sound to treat the letters as abbreviated letters like Ya-Sin or Alif-Lam-Mim, whose meaning is not known, and al-Shinqiti holds this to be the most likely view. Al-Qurtubi and al-Baydawi also mention other readings, such as a name of the Prophet, a name of God or an oath, but most scholars regard them as weak. On the verse 'We did not send down the Qur'an to make you miserable, but as a reminder for whoever fears', al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Kathir explain that the Prophet's duty is to convey and warn, not to force belief. Grammarians disagree on whether 'a reminder' is an apposition, as al-Zajjaj held and Abu 'Ali al-Farisi rejected, or an accusative of purpose or of the verbal noun. Regarding the revelation 'sent down from the One who created the earth and the high heavens', the commentators relate it to God's majesty. On 'He is established on the Throne', Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi follow the view of the early scholars, affirming it without modality or distortion, whereas al-Mawardi and others offer interpretations of the word. All agree that God knows the secret and what is even more hidden, and that His names are the most beautiful.

This verse states that God did not send down the Qur'an to the Prophet ﷺ so that he would suffer or be burdened, but as a reminder for those who fear God. The commentators differ on the meaning of "Ta Ha" at the start. Al-Tabari, followed by many, including Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, 'Ikrimah, al-Hasan and Qatadah, takes it to mean "O man" in a particular language, and al-Kalbi attributes it to the dialect of the tribe of 'Akk. Others see it as a divine name, a name of the Prophet or of the surah, while Ibn 'Atiyya, Abu Hayyan and al-Suyuti consider it one of the disjointed letters. As for "that you should be distressed", most explain it as exhausting effort in worship, such as long night prayers that swelled his feet, and al-Tabari, Mujahid and Muqatil report this as the occasion of revelation. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and Abu al-Su'ud prefer the sense of grief over his people's disbelief, while Ibn Kathir and Qatadah stress that the Qur'an is a mercy and a light. Some report that the polytheists accused him of ruining himself by abandoning his forefathers' religion. Al-Sa'di and al-Sha'rawi emphasise that divine law leads to happiness. The commentators then agree on God's greatness: the Creator of the earth and the lofty heavens, who is established on the Throne, owns all that is in the heavens, on earth and beneath the soil, and knows the secret and what is more hidden still.

The commentators explain that the verse "We did not send down the Quran to you for you to be distressed" means that God did not reveal the Quran to torment His Prophet with hardship or exhaustion, and that "only as a reminder for those who fear" means it was revealed as an admonition for whoever has fear of God in his heart and is moved by the warning. Most agree that the word "shaqa" here means toil and hardship. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report that the Quraysh said Muhammad had become wretched because of this Quran, and that the verse rejects that charge. Mujahid, Ibn Jurayj and al-Tabari also report that the hardship refers to the Prophet's long night prayers, until his feet swelled, while al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya understand it as the burdens of preaching and prophethood, and al-Razi, Abu Hayyan and Abu al-Su'ud see it as consolation for his grief over his people's disbelief. On grammar, al-Zajjaj allowed "reminder" to be an apposition to "that you be distressed," but Abu Ali al-Farisi and al-Zamakhshari rejected this because a reminder is not a hardship, so many read the phrase as an exceptive "but," meaning "rather." Several commentators stress that fear of God is what enables a person to benefit from the reminder. Al-Sa'di, al-Qasimi and others conclude that the Quran places no unbearable burden on believers.

This verse states that the Qur'an is a revelation sent down from the One who created the earth and the lofty heavens. The commentators agree that naming the Creator elevates the Qur'an's status, and that mentioning the creation of earth and heavens points to immense power. They differ on the grammar of the word "tanzilan": al-Tabari treats it as a verbal noun whose verb is implied, while others read it as an appositive or as a term whose role depends on how the sentence is parsed; this does not change the basic meaning. On "the Merciful established Himself upon the Throne," al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir keep the apparent sense without asking how, in the manner of the early scholars, whereas al-Razi and Ibn 'Atiyya interpret istawa as dominion and control, and Ibn 'Ashur sees the Throne as an image of royal majesty. All agree that God owns what is in the heavens, on earth, between them, and under the moist soil, the tharaa. They differ on what lies beneath it: Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Kathir describe lower layers, and several reports cited there are judged weak by some scholars. Finally, the commentators agree that God's knowledge encompasses what is secret and what is even more hidden, and that He alone is God, to whom belong the most beautiful names.

The commentators explain that this verse affirms that the Most Merciful has established Himself upon the Throne, and that istiwa' is understood in Arabic as rising above and being exalted. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Jazairi hold this sense and advise following the wording without qualifying it, distorting it, likening it or denying it. Az-Zamakhshari, Abu Hayyan, al-Nasafi and Abu al-Su'ud instead read the phrase as a figure of speech for kingship and authority, as when one says someone has ascended the throne to mean he rules, even without sitting on it, just as "his hand is outstretched" means he is generous. Al-Razi grants that dominion or power is the closest meaning in the language, while discussing at length the objections to that reading. Ibn 'Ashur places the verse among those whose meaning is clear from Arabic usage while maintaining the transcendence of God. Al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir cite Malik, who said that istiwa' is known, its modality unknown, belief in it obligatory, and asking about it an innovation. All agree on what follows: to God belongs whatever is in the heavens, on the earth, between them and beneath the soil; He knows the secret and what is more hidden still, and He is the only God, to whom belong the most beautiful names.

This verse states that God owns everything in the heavens and the earth, everything between them, and what lies beneath the thara, meaning moist soil. The commentators agree that this ownership covers possession, governance and knowledge. They differ on what lies under the thara. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi understand it as what lies beneath the seven earths, while al-Qurtubi, al-Baghawi and al-Sam'ani report that the thara is the rock beneath the seventh earth. These latter authors cite narrations attributed to Ibn 'Abbas about the earth resting on a fish, a rock and a bull, but Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi and al-Baghawi regard these reports as Israelite material that cannot be relied upon. Al-Razi takes the thara to be the outermost layer of the world and leaves open what lies below it. On the next verse, about the secret and what is more hidden, al-Tabari, Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn Kathir report differing views: the secret is what a person tells himself or confides to others, and the more hidden is what he has not yet thought of. Ibn Zayd and Ibn al-Jawzi even hold that the more hidden is God's own secret, a view al-Tabari rejects. Al-Alusi and al-Baydawi also note the grammatical and reading options for these words. Several exegetes, including al-Sa'di and Sayyid Qutb, observe that the passage reassures the Prophet, showing that God knows him and does not leave him alone.

This passage from Surah Ta-Ha affirms that God knows whatever a person says aloud or in a whisper, and even what is more hidden than a secret. The commentators agree on the plain sense: God's knowledge embraces both spoken and unspoken words, and raising one's voice adds nothing to what He already knows. Ibn Abbas and Sa'id ibn Jubayr explain that the secret is what a person confides to another privately, and what is more hidden is what he says to himself. Mujahid understands the latter as inner whispering (waswasa), while others take it as what a person intends before resolving upon it. Qatada and al-Dahhak read the secret as what one conceals in the heart, and the more hidden as what has not yet occurred but will. Ibn Zayd holds that God knows the secrets of His servants while keeping His own secret hidden, a view al-Tabari rejects in favour of reading the word as a comparative meaning 'more hidden than the secret'. Al-Zamakhshari and others note that the conditional may teach that invoking God aloud is not needed for Him to hear, since He knows it either way. Al-Alusi reports that some scholars addressed the verse to the Prophet and his community, and that some applied it to recitation and supplication. All agree on the lesson of constant awareness of God, in public and in private.

The commentators explain that the verse 'Allah — there is no god but He; to Him belong the most beautiful names' sums up the attributes already mentioned: He alone is the true object of worship, without partner, and His names are the most perfect. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Razi and Ibn 'Ashur agree on this. Al-Tabari notes that 'al-husna' takes the feminine singular because it describes names treated as a group, as in 'other needs'. Al-Razi and al-Zamakhshari add that the beauty of these names lies in their meanings, which express holiness, majesty, lordship and perfect acts. The surrounding verses state that God owns all that is in the heavens and on earth and beneath the moist soil, and that His knowledge embraces both the spoken secret and what is more hidden. Scholars differ on 'al-thara': some take it as moist earth, others as what lies below the seventh earth. On 'akhfa', Ibn 'Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Mujahid take it as what the self has not yet acted upon or spoken, while Ibn Zayd understands it as God's own secret, a view al-Tabari rejects. The meaning of 'Ta-Ha' is also disputed: Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, al-Hasan and 'Ikrima took it as 'O man' in some ancient or foreign tongue, a reading al-Tabari and Ibn 'Atiyya favour, while others offered different explanations without settling the matter. Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi and al-Razi cite hadiths on the divine names and on the surahs, but they note weaknesses in their chains and do not build the meaning on them.

God addresses His Prophet ﷺ, in the form of a question meant to arouse attention, to tell him the story of Moses when he saw a fire on a dark winter night after losing his way. He said to his family: stay here, I have seen a fire; perhaps I will bring you a live coal from it, or find there someone who will guide me. The commentators report that this occurred when Moses had completed the term agreed upon and set out with his family toward Egypt, and that the fire was in truth a light from God. The qabas is an ember at the tip of a stick, and the hudan is, according to Qatada, a guide, while others take it as a sign by which one can find the way. All agree that this account consoles the Prophet and invites him to emulate Moses' patience under the hardships of his mission. They differ on why Moses was told to remove his sandals: some say they were made of the skin of a dead donkey, others say he was to let his feet touch the blessed earth of the valley, and others see it as a sign of humility and reverence. Most take Tuwa to be the name of the valley, and explain that listening to what is revealed means paying attention and understanding, and that prayer is performed in order to remember God. As for 'I am almost about to conceal it', most explain it as 'I conceal it even from myself', while others see in it an exaggeration of secrecy in the Arab manner, and a few consider the word 'almost' to be merely emphatic. The passage concludes with a warning that those who do not believe in the Hour must not turn him away from it, for it will come so that every soul may be recompensed for what it has striven for.

God tells His Prophet ﷺ the story of Moses who, on a cold dark night, having lost his way, saw a fire and told his family to wait: he had seen a fire, and would bring them a brand from it or find someone there to guide him. The commentators agree that the word anasa means to see clearly, that qabas is a lit brand at the tip of a stick or wick, and that huda refers to someone who points out the way. Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada and Mujahid, as reported by al-Tabari, understand that Moses had lost his path and sought a guide, while al-Mawardi, al-Qurtubi and al-Baydawi also allow a religious guidance, which al-Zamakhshari attributes to Mujahid and Qatada. Most exegetes, including al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir, report that what Moses saw was in reality a light which he took for fire; Sa'id ibn Jubayr holds that it was truly a fire, one of God's veils. The reports differ about the tree in which the fire appeared: Ibn Mas'ud says it was a green acacia, Qatada and al-Kalbi a thorny shrub, Wahb a lycium, and Ibn 'Abbas a jujube, while Ibn Kathir prefers not to specify it. Other matters connected with the verse include the removal of the sandals: some explain it by the fact that they were of untanned donkey hide, others by humility or seeking the blessing of the sacred valley, as al-Qurtubi notes. The overall meaning is that this account consoles the Prophet ﷺ and invites him to follow Moses in patience under the burdens of prophethood.

The commentators describe this verse as the opening of the scene in which Moses, having reached the fire he had seen from afar on a cold, dark night, hears the divine call. Ibn Abbas and others report that the fire was in a green tree whose radiance did not dim its greenness, nor did its greenness quench the light. The exegetes agree that the speaker is God, and that the repeated phrase “I am your Lord” serves to affirm the message and remove any doubt. The command to remove the sandals is, for most, a sign of reverence for the place and for the divine speech, like the humility shown before a king. Ali, Ibn Abbas, Ikrima and Qatada report that the sandals were of an unslaughtered dead donkey's hide, whereas al-Hasan, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Mujahid explain that the aim was for his feet to touch the blessing of the sacred valley. As for the word “Tuwa”, al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir take it as the name of the valley, while others read it as meaning “twice”, that is, sanctified twice, or as deriving from folding, meaning traversed by night. Readers also differ on the vowel of “anni” (opened or with a kasra) and on whether “Tuwa” takes tanwin.

The commentators explain that God called Moses from the bush blazing with light in the sacred valley, revealing Himself as his Lord and ordering him to take off his sandals as a mark of respect for the place where God speaks, since he was in the purified valley. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Qurtubi agree that this command expresses reverence and humility before God, and that “sacred” means purified and blessed. On the reason for the gesture, opinions differ: Ali ibn Abi Talib, Ka'b, 'Ikrima and Qatada, and Ibn Mas'ud as cited by Ibn al-Jawzi, hold that the sandals were made of the skin of a dead donkey, which had to be removed as impure, whereas al-Hasan, Mujahid and Sa'id ibn Jubayr say they were of ritually slaughtered cow hide and that the aim was for his feet to touch the blessed ground. Al-Tabari prefers the second view, while Ibn 'Atiyya considers the sense of humility during the divine address more fitting, a view shared by al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Ashur. As for the word “Tuwa”, the main reading is that it is the name of the valley, according to Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and most exegetes; others take it to mean “twice”, either that the valley was sanctified twice or that Moses was called twice, as al-Zamakhshari and al-Qurtubi note. The readings differ in vowelling and tanwin without substantially changing the meaning. The following verses report that God chose Moses, commanded him to affirm monotheism and to perform prayer in remembrance of Him, and declared that the Hour is certain; its time has been concealed so that every soul is repaid for its deeds, and warns against being turned away from faith by those who follow their desires.

In this verse God tells Moses that He has chosen him for His mission and commands him to listen carefully to what is revealed to him. The commentators agree that the choice refers to his election to prophethood and messengership, and that the listening required is full attention of heart, mind and body, not merely hearing. Al-Baghawi and Abu Hayyan describe the etiquette of listening as stillness of the limbs, lowered gaze, presence of mind and resolve to act. Most of them identify the revelation as the sentence that follows: 'I am God; there is no god but Me; so worship Me', which states the oneness of God as the foundation of the message. The grammarians differ on how the phrase 'to what is revealed' is linked. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi connect it either to 'listen' or to 'I have chosen you', while Abu Hayyan connects it to 'listen', since linking it to the second verb would require a construction he considers impermissible. Al-Tabari observes that the two readings, 'wa-anā' and 'wa-annā', both carry the same meaning, and that Hamza read 'wa-innā ikhtarnāka' in the plural of majesty. The commentators agree that this choice is a great honour that calls for gratitude and attentive listening.

God tells Moses that He is Allah, the only deity worthy of worship, and commands him to worship Him alone and establish prayer in remembrance of Him. The commentators agree that the core of the faith is monotheism and that prayer is its highest form. They differ on the meaning of "for My remembrance": al-Tabari, Mujahid, Ibn Kathir and al-Nasafi take it as "so that you remember Me in it", since prayer contains invocations, while Ibrahim al-Nakha'i and Ibn Juzayy read it as "at the time you remember it", relying on the hadith that a missed prayer should be prayed when one recalls it. Al-Tabari and Ibn 'Atiyya prefer the first meaning as the more apparent, while al-Razi lists several other senses, such as sincerity in remembrance. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi explain that prayer is singled out for its excellence among acts of worship, and Ibn 'Ashur understands establishing prayer as maintaining it without neglect. On the statement that the Hour is coming, the commentators agree that its exact time is hidden from creation. For "I almost conceal it", Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatada and Ibn Kathir explain "I conceal it even from myself", al-Akhfash and al-Nahhas read it as "I intend to conceal it", and Ibn al-Anbari takes the sentence as broken off. Sa'id ibn Jubayr's reading "ukhfiha" is cited as meaning "I reveal it". The purpose of this concealment is that people act without knowing when it will come. God also warns Moses not to let anyone who disbelieves and follows his desires turn him away from it, for such a person will perish.

This verse declares that the Hour, meaning the Resurrection when people are raised for judgement, is certainly coming, and that God almost conceals its timing, to the point, the commentators say, of hiding it even from Himself. The view most scholars give is that its time is hidden from all creation, so that every soul may be repaid for what it did, good or bad. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatada and Ibn Kathir, along with most exegetes, read 'I almost hide it from myself' as an Arabic idiom of extreme secrecy, and Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi note that some codices add 'how would I show it to you'. Al-Akhfash, Ibn al-Anbari and Abu Muslim take 'kada' to mean 'to intend', while others treat it as an emphatic particle or as a verb with an omitted predicate. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn 'Ashur also record the reading of Sa'id ibn Jubayr, 'akhfiha' meaning 'to reveal it', which they accept linguistically but regard as less established. Al-Razi, al-Baydawi and Ibn 'Ashur favour the sense of approaching: God nearly refrains from announcing that the Hour is coming. The clause 'so that every soul may be repaid' attaches to the Hour, and 'sa'y' means one's deeds, good or evil. The verse then warns Moses not to be turned from belief in the Hour by those who deny it and follow their desires, since that leads to ruin; al-Razi and al-Zamakhshari note that the pronoun 'it' may refer to the prayer rather than the Hour, though most take it to mean the Hour.

The commentators connect this verse with the preceding statement that the Hour is coming, and read it as a warning: let not someone who does not believe in it and follows his desire turn you away from it and from preparing for it, lest you perish. They differ on what the pronouns refer to. Ibn 'Abbas and most exegetes take them to mean the Hour; Abu Muslim and others take the first to mean the prayer, and some take it to mean the testimony that there is no god but God. As for the addressee, most say it is Moses, while al-Naqqash held it was the Prophet Muhammad, which Ibn 'Atiyya considered very far-fetched. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi argue that the prohibition, outwardly addressed to the disbeliever, is really addressed to the speaker himself, like the saying «I do not want to see you here»; it calls for firmness in faith and for reasoning from evidence rather than imitation. Ibn Kathir reads it as a general admonition to every believer. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Baydawi note that «fatardā» is in the subjunctive after the prohibition, meaning «you would perish». All agree that the core message is a warning against heedlessness of the Hour and the pursuit of desire, whose end is ruin.

God asks Moses what is in his right hand. The commentators explain that this is a question of confirmation rather than real inquiry: it is meant to make Moses affirm that it is a staff, so that when it turns into a serpent the miracle is clearly recognized. Moses replies that it is his staff, which he leans on, with which he knocks down leaves from the branches for his flock, and which serves him for other purposes. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi agree that the word hashsha means striking branches so the leaves fall, and that ma'arib means needs or benefits. Al-Mawardi, al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi list further uses, such as a hook, a fork for carrying loads, and defence against wild animals. Ibn Kathir considers that many of the wonders attributed to the staff belong to Israelite narratives and are not reliable. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Atiyya suggest that Moses gave a summary of its uses, perhaps to prolong the conversation with God. Some readings are discussed, such as the variant with sin attributed to Ikrima, and the grammar of the demonstrative. Al-Razi adds that the question serves to reassure Moses and calm his awe before the divine speech.

Moses tells his Lord that what is in his right hand is his staff, on which he leans while walking, standing or when tired, and with which he strikes the branches so that their leaves fall for his sheep to eat. He adds that the staff has other uses for him. Most commentators understand the word "ma'arib" as needs and benefits. Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Qatada and others say these are various needs, and al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi list them: carrying provisions and a water-skin, tying a rope and drawing water from a well, killing snakes, driving wild beasts away from the flock, and sheltering under it. The details are not agreed upon. Some report that the staff gave light at night and guarded the flock, but Ibn Kathir considers this Israelite narration, arguing that Moses would not have been startled by its transformation had he known such powers. As to the staff itself, Muqatil says it was of nabaa wood, Wahb says it came from the myrtle of Paradise, and others name the milkweed. In recitation, Ikrima reads "ahassu" with a sin, which some take to mean driving the flock, while others say the two forms are synonyms. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and Abu Hayyan offer several reasons for God's question, though He knows the answer: to establish proof, to reassure Moses, or to prepare him for the miracle. Al-Razi also notes that Moses kept his answer brief, hoping God would ask about the other uses so that the conversation would continue.

God commands Moses to throw down the staff in his hand, and it at once becomes a huge serpent moving swiftly. The commentators explain that this transformation was an extraordinary sign granted by God to confirm Moses' prophethood, and that the word hayya covers both small and large serpents, male and female. They agree that the command was meant to show Moses a proof that would support his mission before Pharaoh. They differ, however, on the serpent's description. Ibn 'Abbas, Wahb ibn Munabbih and al-Kalbi describe it as yellow and so large that it swallowed rocks and trees, while al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and Ibn Kathir explain that the word jann refers to its initial state and thu'ban to its final one. Al-Baydawi notes that these names reflect the different stages of its form. Ibn Kathir and al-Sa'di report that Moses was frightened and fled, that God called him back and told him to take it, and that it returned to being a staff. Abu Hayyan observes that the command follows a question meant to establish the fact. The commentators present these views without judging between them.

The commentators explain that Moses threw the staff he held in his right hand, at God's command, and it immediately became a serpent moving swiftly on its belly. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Baydawi agree that this was a miracle from God that no one but God could perform. They differ on the serpent's nature. Al-Tabari and Ibn Abbas, followed by several others, report that it first was a small yellow snake that then swelled into a large serpent, which explains why it is called jann in one place and tha'ban in another. Al-Zamakhshari holds instead that it was a large serpent from the start, with the speed of a jann. Ibn Kathir cites Israelite reports about its great size and about how it swallowed rocks and trees, but judges such reports unreliable, and others do not adopt them. As for the phrase that God will return it to its former state, most understand that it would become a staff again. Al-Razi, al-Mawardi and Ibn Atiyya explain that the sign was a clear proof of Moses' mission and reassured him before he faced Pharaoh. Several note that Moses was seized with fear and fled, before God told him to take hold of it without fear.

God tells Moses to take the serpent his staff has become and not to fear it, for He will return it to its original form as a staff. The commentators agree on the plain meaning: the staff will be restored to its first state, and the command to seize it was meant to calm Moses and train him for his mission. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Qatada explain the word sira as referring to the original shape or condition, a view al-Tabari transmits, while al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi note that the word can also mean a way of acting and that the verb may be read as taking the form of an adverbial phrase. Several detailed accounts, quoted by al-Baghawi, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir, describe Moses hesitating, wrapping his hand in the sleeve of his woollen garment, and being rebuked by an angel; Ibn Kathir however considers much of this to come from Israelite narratives. Al-Razi observes that fear is a natural human reaction to such a sight and does not weaken prophethood, while others link it to Moses' knowledge of what the serpent did to Adam. The shared purpose of the commentators is that Moses should be given a clear proof before standing before Pharaoh, and that this sign was meant to prepare him for the later miracles.

This verse tells Moses to draw his hand against his side, under the arm, so that it comes out white and shining, without any leprosy. It is a second sign, following the staff turning into a serpent. The commentators agree that the word "sواوa" here means leprosy, and that the whiteness is a light like the sun's, as reported from Ibn Abbas, Qatada and Mujahid. On the meaning of "janah", al-Tabari and Mujahid take it to be the upper arm, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Juzayy the side, Ibn Abbas the chest, and al-Razi prefers the side because the hand resembles a bird's wing. Ibn Kathir sees in this gesture the second proof described elsewhere, where the hand is put into the collar. Al-Zamakhshari praises the Qur'an's delicate way of naming leprosy without stating it. Most exegetes hold that the two signs together are among the greatest signs. Al-Hasan considers the hand greater than the staff, a view al-Razi rejects, noting that the staff changed far more. The verse then leads to Moses being sent to Pharaoh, who has transgressed, which most explain as his claim to divinity.

The commentators explain that this verse follows the sign of the staff: God tells Moses to draw his hand against his side, beneath the arm, so that it comes out white without any affliction, as a second sign. Most agree that "without blemish" means without leprosy, and that the word "blemish" is a euphemism for leprosy, just as the private parts are referred to by a veiled term, as al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and Abu Hayyan note. They differ on the particle "that We may show you". Al-Zamakhshari and those who follow him take it to govern an implied verb, meaning that We did this so that We might show you, while others attach it to the verb "come out" or to the sense of the passage. The phrase "of Our greatest signs" may describe the signs or be the object of the verb to show; Abu Hayyan and others treat it as an adjective of the signs, and Ibn Kathir reports that Moses' hand shone like a lamp. Ibn Abbas holds that the hand was his greatest sign, while al-Hasan al-Basri judges the hand greater than the staff; al-Razi replies that the staff involved more transformations. Commentators also explain the feminine form "greatest" instead of the masculine by the need to match the rhyme of the verses, by an implied word, or by an inversion of word order.

God commands Moses to go to Pharaoh because he has transgressed all limits in disbelief and rebellion, to the point of claiming divinity. The command is therefore to call him to worship the One God and to let the Children of Israel go with Moses. The commentators agree on the meaning of tughyan: going beyond the proper measure, rebelling and acting with arrogance. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Nasafi and al-Baydawi explain that the tyrant overstepped the limits of servanthood by claiming lordship. Ibn 'Ashur notes that the mission is a specific one, namely to tell him to stop worshipping other than God, and that Moses understood this aim from the signs shown to him. Al-Razi and al-Jalalayn explain that Pharaoh is singled out because he is the head of disbelief and his people follow him. Al-Razi, Ibn Kathir and al-Tha'alibi relay, through Wahb ibn Munabbih, divine words that reassure Moses, though not all scholars accept these accounts. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi observe that such a mission requires great steadfastness of heart, which explains Moses's request that follows. Ibn Sa'di adds that God punishes no one until the messengers have established the proof against them. The commentators do not judge between these views, and their differences mainly concern the details of the story.

In this verse Moses asks his Lord to expand his chest, meaning to make his heart broader and steadier so that he can bear the weight of the mission and the hardships of calling Pharaoh, and to make his task easy. The commentators agree that expanding the chest here means firmness, calm and the capacity to endure insult and hardship. Ibn Zayd understood it as boldness, while al-Kirmani and al-Nasafi understood it as readiness to receive revelation and bear the burdens of preaching. Al-Razi links it to the light of knowledge and inner tranquillity. Al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan take the word 'for me' as emphasis, while Ibn 'Ashur sees it as showing that the benefit returns to Moses himself. Regarding the knot in his tongue, the commentators agree that it was an impediment caused, according to al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir, by a live coal placed in his mouth as a child; Ibn Juzayy mentions the same story. They differ on whether it was fully removed. Al-Hasan and Ibn Kathir held that it was removed, citing 'you have been granted your request', whereas al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and Abu Hayyan held that a trace remained, citing Pharaoh's words that he 'hardly speaks clearly'. Al-Razi answers that this means he cannot bring an argument. All agree that the purpose was to be understood. Finally, Moses asks for his brother Aaron as a helper, who was more eloquent and older, to strengthen him in his mission.

In this verse Moses asks his Lord to expand his chest, meaning to strengthen him to bear the weight of his mission and the trials of confronting Pharaoh, and to make his task easy. Al-Tabari, citing Ibn Zayd, explains the expansion as boldness, while Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi stress patience and steadiness under hardship, and al-Razi understands it as a light and tranquillity that let him retain the revelation. On making the task easy, most commentators take it as providing the means to deliver the message; al-Razi notes that the Ash'aris see it as God creating the will and power, while the Mu'tazilites speak of favours that move the agent to act, and he leaves the matter there. Several reports, notably those cited by al-Tabari and al-Baghawi, link the request to Moses's fear of Pharaoh's people after the killing and to a speech impediment caused by a burning coal placed in his mouth in childhood. He asks that the knot be loosened so that he may be understood. Al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir record that some held the impediment fully removed, while others held that some of it remained, and Ibn Kathir considers al-Hasan al-Basri's view that it was completely removed weak, because Moses asked only for part of the knot to be undone. He then asks for a wazir from his family, his brother Aaron, to support him and share his mission. The commentators explain that a wazir bears part of a ruler's burden and gives counsel. He ends by stating that the purpose of this help is to glorify and remember God abundantly, and that God is fully aware of their condition.

In these verses Moses asks his Lord to open his chest so that he can bear the weight of his mission and to make his task easy, to loosen the knot in his tongue so that people can understand him, and to give him a helper from his family, his brother Harun, to strengthen his back and share in his affair. The commentators explain the knot as a speech impediment caused by an ember he had placed in his mouth as a child, when Pharaoh wanted to kill him. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report that Moses did not ask for the whole impediment to vanish, only enough to be understood, while al-Hasan al-Basri held that the knot was entirely removed, citing the verse, you have been given your request, O Moses. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Jubba'i held that part of it remained, relying on Pharaoh's words and on Moses' statement that his brother is more eloquent than he. Al-Razi and Ibn al-Jawzi explain that opening the chest means widening it so it can endure hardship. The word wazir is derived by scholars either from bearing a burden or from giving support, and the verbs are read mainly as prayers, while Ibn Amir's reading in the first person suggests that the request concerns assistance in the task rather than prophethood. The verses end with the aim that the two brothers glorify and remember God much, and with the reminder that God sees them.

In these verses Moses asks his Lord to expand his chest, meaning to strengthen him to bear the weight of his mission and the trials of confronting Pharaoh, to make his task easy, and to loosen the knot in his tongue so that the people may understand his speech. The commentators explain that this knot was a speech impediment: Ibn Abbas calls it a lisp, and al-Tabari, Mujahid, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Muqatil and al-Baghawi relate the story of the ember Moses placed in his mouth as a child after pulling Pharaoh's beard. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi read the request as aiming at being understood rather than at perfect eloquence. On whether the impediment was removed, opinions differ. al-Hasan and others hold that it was fully lifted, citing the verse 'you have been granted your request, O Moses', while al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and Ibn Kathir hold that part of it remained, citing 'my brother Aaron is more eloquent than I' and Pharaoh's remark that he 'can hardly make himself clear'. Al-Razi and al-Alusi reply that Pharaoh's remark denies the ability to argue and prove, not speech in general. Moses then asks for a minister from his own family, his brother Aaron, to support him and share his mission, and al-Razi notes that Aaron was the older. Ibn Ashur and al-Biqa'i connect these requests to the stated aim of glorifying and remembering God abundantly, and read the closing phrase as an appeal grounded in God's knowledge of their condition.

In this verse Moses asks his Lord to appoint for him a helper from his family to share the burden of his mission, and he names his brother Aaron. The commentators agree that the wazir is one who bears part of the load of the one he assists and on whom he can rely, that Aaron was older than Moses, and that he was more eloquent. Ibn Abbas, transmitted by al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir, adds that Moses asked that Aaron also be made a prophet. For the phrase 'strengthen my back through him', al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baydawi understand support and reinforcement, while al-Razi, citing Abu Ubayda, takes it literally as the back. On the etymology of wazir, al-Zajjaj and al-Baghawi connect it to burden or refuge, al-Asma'i to mutual aid, and al-Zamakhshari proposes an original form azir whose hamza became a waw. Al-Tabari and al-Razi note that Moses' speech impediment, caused by an ember in childhood, made such help necessary. According to Ibn Kathir, al-Baydawi and al-Baghawi, the purpose of the request is that Moses and Aaron may glorify and remember God abundantly.

Moses asks his Lord to expand his chest, to ease his task, to loosen a knot from his tongue so that his people may understand his speech, and to give him a helper from his family, his brother Harun, to strengthen his back and share in his mission. Commentators explain that expanding the chest means making it able to bear the burden of prophethood and Pharaoh's hardness, and easing the task means removing obstacles. As for the knot, al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and others report that it came from an ember Moses put in his mouth as a child when he seized Pharaoh's beard; al-Razi notes that others took it to be a congenital impediment. Al-Hasan al-Basri held that the knot was wholly undone, while others, citing Pharaoh's remark that he can hardly speak clearly, held that some of it remained. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi observe that Moses asked only for part of the knot to be loosened, not for full eloquence. On the word wazir, the scholars give several derivations: from the burden (wizr) a minister carries, from a refuge (wazar) on which the ruler relies, or from mutual support (muwazara). Ibn 'Abbas said Harun was the elder. Ibn 'Amir reads the verbs as first-person responses, while the majority read them as imperatives in the form of a prayer. Moses gives as his reason that they may glorify and remember God often, for He sees them.

In these verses Moses asks his Lord to strengthen his back through his brother, meaning to support and reinforce him. The commentators broadly agree on this meaning: al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi explain that the word azr means the back or strength, and that to help someone is to make him strong. They report that Moses asks that Aaron become his minister (wazir) and helper in the mission to Pharaoh, and that he be associated with his affair, namely prophethood. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and Ibn Atiyya explain that the word wazir may derive from the root meaning burden (wizr), from the root meaning refuge (wazar), or from mutual aid (muwazara), and that its original form would have been azir. Ibn Amir alone reads the verbs ashdid and ashrikhu in the imperfect, as a response to the request, while the general reading is in the imperative. Al-Tabari judges this reading possible but not preferred. Moses justifies his request by saying that he and his brother will glorify God and remember Him abundantly, and several exegetes, including Ibn Kathir and al-Sa'di, explain that 'You have always been aware of us' means that God knows their situation and need. Al-Razi and Ibn Ashur note that Aaron was older than Moses and more eloquent.

In this verse Moses asks his Lord to strengthen his back through his brother Aaron and to make him a partner in his mission and prophethood. The commentators explain that the purpose is that they may glorify God and remember Him abundantly, since God knows their state and need. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi understand the word azr as strength or the back, and the shared matter as prophethood and conveying the message. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi note that the request also made Aaron a minister who would share the burden. Al-Razi adds that Moses did not ask for the full removal of his speech impediment, only enough to be understood, while Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi connect the impediment to a burn from childhood, as narrated through Ibn Abbas. On the reading, al-Tabari and most readers take the verbs as imperatives in the form of a supplication, whereas Ibn Amir reads them as a statement by Moses about his own action, a reading al-Tabari considers less well-founded. Al-Razi and Ibn Ashur see here a sign of the value of cooperation in calling to God, and al-Razi holds that remembrance and glorification are the ultimate aim.

In these verses Moses asks his Lord to expand his chest, ease his task, loosen the knot in his tongue, and give him his brother Harun as a helper to strengthen him and share his mission. The stated purpose, as the verse says, is that they glorify God abundantly and remember Him abundantly. Commentators explain that glorification (tasbih) means declaring God free of what is unfitting for Him, that some also take it to mean prayer, and that remembrance (dhikr) means praising God for His blessings. Most, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi, read the phrase 'You have always been watchful over us' as God's knowledge of their situation and of how mutual support benefits them; others take it to mean that God has watched over them since childhood. On the knot in the tongue, opinions differ. Ibn Abbas and Mujahid trace it to the ember placed in his mouth as a child, while others hold it was a natural impediment. Al-Hasan says only one knot was loosened, whereas others say it was removed entirely, citing 'you have been granted your request', and those who rely on Pharaoh's words 'he can barely speak clearly' hold that some trace remained. Al-Razi notes that the request concerned being understood, not perfect eloquence. On Harun's role, the commentators agree he was to support and strengthen Moses in conveying the message, but they disagree on whether 'sharing the matter' meant prophethood or simple assistance. Ibn Ashur also notes that the two readings of the imperative and the jussive differ in grammar and meaning.

The commentators explain that after Moses was commanded to go to Pharaoh, he asked his Lord to expand his chest, ease his task, loosen the knot in his tongue so that people would understand his speech, and give him his brother Aaron as a helper and partner in the mission. The purpose, they agree, is that the two of them may glorify and remember God abundantly, for He sees their condition. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Abi Hatim take the word azr to mean back or strength, and the partnership in the matter to mean prophethood and delivering the message. The commentators differ on whether the knot in his tongue was fully removed. Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan and Mujahid link it to the ember placed in his mouth in childhood, and al-Hasan holds that God loosened only one knot in answer to the prayer. Al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan conclude that some impediment remained, citing Pharaoh's words that he hardly speaks clearly, whereas al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir find this argument unconvincing, and al-Razi says the aim was comprehension rather than perfect eloquence. Most explain wazir as derived from wizr (burden) or mu'azara (assistance). Ibn Amir reads the verbs in the indicative, a reading Ibn Atiyya and al-Nahhas consider weak. Al-Razi explains that glorification is placed first because it belongs to the heart, while remembrance belongs to the tongue; most take glorification as declaring God free of imperfections and remembrance as praising Him.
