In these verses Moses asks his Lord to expand his chest, to make his task easy, to loosen a knot in his tongue so that his people may understand him, and to give him a minister from his family, his brother Aaron, to strengthen his back and share in his mission. He adds that this support will help them glorify God and remember Him abundantly, and he ends with the words "Indeed You are ever Seeing of us", meaning that You know our condition.

The commentators agree that "strengthen my back through him" means to reinforce my support and help me, as al-Tabari reports from Ibn Abbas and Ibn Zayd. Al-Mawardi and al-Zamakhshari note that azr can mean strength, the back, or aid, and that the Arabs say "azarahu" for "he strengthened him". On the word "basir", al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi explain it as knowing and informed, while al-Qurtubi notes that it can also mean one who sees and one who knows hidden matters.

As for the knot in the tongue, Ibn Abbas and several exegetes take it as an impediment of speech caused by the live coal Moses placed in his mouth as a child. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi observe that he asked for part of the knot to be loosed, so that he could be understood, not for perfect eloquence. Al-Hasan held instead that the whole knot was removed, a view others contest by citing Pharaoh's remark that he can hardly speak clearly.

Al-Razi, Ibn Atiyya and al-Zamakhshari explain that the word "wazir" derives from burden, refuge, or mutual aid. Some understand Aaron's association as a request that he share in prophethood, while others take it as support in the mission only. The readings differ on the verbs "ushdud" and "ashrik": the majority read them as supplications, while Ibn Amir reads them as conditional responses, a reading several scholars consider less likely.

The commentators explain that God grants Moses what he asked for: the expansion of his chest, the ease of his task, the loosening of the knot in his tongue, and the appointment of his brother Aaron as a minister and partner in the mission. God says to him: you have been given what you asked, O Moses. Most agree that the word su'l (request) here means the thing requested, like khubz (bread) meaning what is baked. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi, Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Atiyya note that this gift is a reminder of earlier favours: God saved him from death when He inspired his mother to place him in the chest and set it on the river, returned him to her, and tested him with several trials from which He delivered him. All agree that 'another time' means an earlier occasion than this request. On the love (mahabba) God cast upon Moses, opinions differ: Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada and 'Ikrima take it to mean the affection people felt for him and his beauty, al-Tabari takes it as divine mercy, Ibn Zayd takes it as the affection of Pharaoh and Asiya, who protected him, and Ibn 'Atiyya judges that the strongest view is acceptance. On the inspiration given to Moses' mother, some speak of inspiration, others of a dream or a messenger, and al-Razi holds she was not a prophet. On the phrase 'under My eye', Qatada explains it as 'nourished by My will', others as 'raised under My watch'. The verse thus combines the answering of the prayer with a reminder of God's earlier grace.

In this verse God reminds Moses that He had bestowed on him another favour, distinct from the one He has just granted to his request. The commentators agree that this favour was Moses' deliverance from Pharaoh, who had ordered the sons of the Children of Israel to be slain. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi understand the inspiration (wahy) given to Moses' mother as an inner inspiration, while al-Razi and al-Baydawi also allow that it may have been a dream, the message of an angel, or a prophet of her time, and Ibn Kathir notes that several scholars held she was not a prophetess. Ibn Abbas and others report that this inspiration guided her to place the child in a chest and set it adrift on the river.

The scholars differ on the phrase "I cast upon you love from Me." Al-Tabari takes it to mean Divine mercy, Ibn Abbas, Qatada and Ikrima take it to mean beauty or charm that drew everyone who saw him, while Ibn Atiyya and al-Zamakhshari take it to mean acceptance, which Ibn Atiyya considers the strongest view. As for "that you may be raised under My eye," al-Baghawi, Qatada and Ibn Kathir explain it as Divine protection and care.

The commentators then recount Moses' successive trials, which they link to the word "futun". Ibn Abbas reads it as a series of tribulations from which God rescued him, Qatada as a testing, and Mujahid as a purification. Al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir mention his return to his mother, and then his stay with Shu'ayb in Madyan.

This verse reminds Moses of an earlier favour from God: the inspiration given to his mother at a time when Pharaoh was killing the newborn boys of the Children of Israel. The commentators explain that she was inspired to place him in a chest and cast him into the river, so that the water would carry him to the bank where the enemy of God and of Moses would take him. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn al-Jawzi and others relate the details, including the sealing of the chest with pitch and its launch on the Nile. Most exegetes, among them al-Razi, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir, understand this as inspiration (ilham), like the inspiration given to the bee, not as prophetic revelation, since they hold that Moses' mother was not a prophet. Others, as Ibn 'Atiyya reports, held that she was a prophetess, that it was a dream, or that an angel came to her without prophetic status, as with Mary; al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and al-Alusi mention these views. On the phrase 'what was revealed', most take the vagueness as a way of magnifying the matter, which is then spelled out, while some say it means what can only be known through revelation. All agree on the central point: God reminds Moses that He watched over him from his birth.

The commentators explain that God reminds Moses of an earlier favour: He inspired his mother to place him in a chest and cast it into the river, the Nile, so that the waters would carry it to the bank where Pharaoh, God's enemy and Moses' enemy, would take him. God then cast upon him a love from Himself, meaning that He made him beloved in people's hearts. As for the phrase 'that you might be reared under My eye', the commentators take it to mean that he would be nourished and raised under divine protection and watch. Most agree that this love is the affection people felt on seeing him: Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada and 'Ikrima state that everyone who saw him loved him. Ibn Zayd reports that Pharaoh loved him and that Asiya, Pharaoh's wife, adopted him. Al-Tabari prefers the meaning of mercy that God placed in hearts. Ibn 'Atiyya holds that the strongest view is acceptance, the favour that God places upon the chosen servants. Al-Zamakhshari and others read 'under My eye' as an image of care and guardianship, while Qatada reads it as being nourished according to God's will. The majority reading is wa-litusna'a with the taa vowelled, which Tabari regards as the only acceptable reading. The passage then continues with Moses returning to his mother, the accidental killing and the trial in Midian, as the commentators recount.

These verses recall the favours God bestowed on Moses in his childhood and youth: He returned him to his mother after he had fallen into the hands of Pharaoh's people, so that she would be comforted and not grieve; He rescued him from distress after he had killed a man by mistake; He tested him with successive trials; then he dwelt among the people of Madyan for years, and finally he came at the appointed measure for his mission. The commentators agree that futun means trial and testing, and that deliverance from distress means safety from being killed and from God's punishment for that killing. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report that Moses' sister pointed Pharaoh's people to the mother who could nurse him, and that Sa'id ibn Jubayr asked Ibn 'Abbas about the fitna, whereupon Ibn 'Abbas listed the successive ordeals from Moses' birth until his flight to Madyan. Al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir also cite Wahb, who said he stayed with Shu'ayb for twenty-eight years. Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn Juzayy take futun as repeated deliverance from ordeals, while al-Tabari links it to the idea of trial. On qadar, Mujahid understands an appointed time, Qatada the measure of prophethood and mission, and Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Kaysan the time when prophets receive revelation, namely forty years of age. As for the love God placed upon Moses, al-Tabari takes it as divine mercy, while Ibn Zayd reports that it was the reason Pharaoh and Asiya protected him. The commentators agree that these verses affirm God's care for Moses at every stage of his life.

The commentators explain that God tells Moses that He has chosen and singled him out for Himself, meaning for His revelation and the delivery of His message. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Juzayy understand this as selection for prophethood and nearness to God, while al-Zamakhshari and al-Alusi read it as an image drawn from a king who keeps a favoured courtier close as a confidant. Al-Zajjaj, quoted by al-Baghawi and al-Nasafi, adds that Moses becomes the intermediary between God and His creatures, as if God Himself were addressing them. Several scholars, including al-Mawardi, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Qurtubi, give the verb isṭana'a the sense of making, shaping, or bestowing favour, which fits the idea of a care that God personally undertook. Al-Razi and Abu al-Su'ud observe that God, who needs nothing, uses the phrase "for Myself" to express the closeness and devotion expected of Moses. Ibn 'Ashur links the verse to the series of favours, including Moses' protection as a child and his stay in Madyan. There is no major disagreement on the overall sense, only on the shade of meaning between election, benefit and closeness. The following words, which order Moses and Aaron to go to Pharaoh without slackening in remembering God, are understood by all as the purpose of this choosing.

God commands Moses and his brother Aaron to go to Pharaoh with His signs and not to slacken in remembering Him. Most commentators, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi, understand the word tanyā as meaning to become weak, falter or grow lax, and relate from Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and Qatada that the verse tells them not to weaken. They explain that remembrance of God gives them strength and steadiness against Pharaoh, whom the verse describes as having transgressed. Al-Suddi and Ibn Abbas, as reported by al-Baghawi, add the sense of not delaying, while Ibn Zayd reads the lax person as one who neglects his duty. Al-Zamakhshari, Abu Hayyan and al-Razi also note that remembrance may mean the transmission of the message, since dhikr covers all acts of worship and that task is the greatest of them.

As for the gentle speech, many commentators take it as courtesy in address. Al-Suddi and Ikrima report that the two men called Pharaoh by a kunya, Abu al-Abbas or Abu al-Walid, and al-Mawardi mentions further kunyas. Muqatil links the gentle word to the invitation to purify oneself and be guided to one's Lord, while others cite promises of enduring youth and undiminished kingship. Al-Razi and al-Baghawi explain the command by Pharaoh's upbringing of Moses, and note that harshness tends to make tyrants more arrogant. Several scholars, including al-Razi and Ibn Atiyya, understand the word la'alla, perhaps, as expressing the hope of the messengers rather than any uncertainty in God.

God commands Moses and his brother Aaron to go to Pharaoh with His signs and not to slacken in remembering Him, since that remembrance strengthens them for their mission. The reason given is that Pharaoh has transgressed all bounds by claiming divinity. The commentators agree that the gentle speech means soft and courteous words without harshness, and that the word 'perhaps' expresses the hope of the two messengers rather than any doubt on God's part. They differ, however, on what this gentle speech consisted of. Ibn Abbas, Ikrima, al-Suddi and Ibn Kathir report that it meant addressing him by a kunya such as Abu al-Abbas or Abu al-Walid. Muqatil, Ibn Mas'ud, al-Baydawi and al-Shawkani identify it with the words: 'Would you purify yourself, and that I guide you to your Lord so that you fear Him?' Others, such as al-Suddi, mention promises of lasting youth and kingship, while al-Hasan takes it as a reminder of a Lord, a return, a paradise and a fire. As for the signs, Ibn Abbas and al-Suddi name the staff and the hand, while others speak of the nine signs. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain 'do not slacken' as weakness or languor, whereas al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi understand it as delivering the message. All report that God reassured them, saying He was with them, hearing and seeing.

This verse commands Moses and Aaron to speak to Pharaoh in gentle words, hoping he will be reminded and heed, or fear and hold back. The commentators agree that gentleness in speech is an effective means of calling people to God, since it softens stubbornness rather than provoking defiance. They differ, however, on what the gentle word was. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Suddi and Ikrima held that it was the use of a kunya, addressing him as Abu al-'Abbas, Abu al-Walid or Abu Murra, and some noted that Pharaoh had three such kunyas. Muqatil, Ibn Kathir and others identified it with the words in Surat al-Nazi'at: Would you purify yourself, and that I guide you to your Lord so that you fear Him? Al-Suddi also reported a promise of youth that never ages and a kingship lasting until death, while al-Hasan al-Basri saw it as telling him that he has a Lord, a return, and a paradise and a fire. On the particle la'alla, Sibawayh and al-Zamakhshari took it as the hope of Moses and Aaron, though God knew Pharaoh would not believe; al-Farra' rendered it as "so that", and others as a question. Several reports say Pharaoh did remember and fear when drowning, but that this did not benefit him. Ibn Kathir and others draw from the verse a lesson in gentle da'wa even toward the most arrogant.

This verse reports the fear of Moses and Aaron when they were commanded to go to Pharaoh. They feared that he would hasten to punish them before they had delivered the message and established the proof, or that his tyranny would increase and he would overstep the limits against them. The commentators broadly agree that the verb yafruṭa means to hasten or to strike first with punishment, and yaṭghā means to exceed bounds or transgress. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report these meanings from Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and Qatada, while Ibn Zayd understood it as fear of immediate punishment before the message was delivered. Al-Mawardi and al-Baghawi add that the root may also mean excess or extravagance, and that yaṭghā may mean killing. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn Atiyya and Abu Hayyan note that the Quran leaves the object of the verb unstated, out of courtesy toward God and to avoid naming what Pharaoh might say. Al-Razi and Abu al-Su'ud observe that fear does not contradict steadfastness, and that God reassured them by promising His presence, protection and attentive watch, since He hears and sees all. Some readers vowel the verb as yufrita, meaning to exceed in harm, and others as yufraṭa, meaning to be driven to haste. The commentators draw from this a lesson of humility: even prophets feel fear and seek reassurance from their Lord.

The commentators explain that God reassured Moses and Aaron when they feared that Pharaoh might strike them with punishment before they delivered the message, or that he might become more tyrannical toward them. God told them not to fear, for He is with them, hearing and seeing. Most exegetes understand this presence as protection, support and help, and the two verbs, hearing and seeing, mean that nothing between them and Pharaoh escapes God's knowledge. Al-Zamakhshari argues that a protector who hears and sees completes his protection and removes concern about the enemy, while Ibn 'Atiyya and others treat the verbs as intransitive because the point is that nothing is hidden from God. As for the word yafrut, Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Ibn Kathir take it to mean hastening punishment or lashing out at them, al-Tabari and al-Zajjaj speak of hastening punishment, and al-Mawardi and al-Qurtubi note that the different readings all converge on excess in harming them. The word tughyan is read by some as killing and by others as crossing the limit in insult. Several scholars, including al-Razi, observe that natural fear does not conflict with prophethood and that tranquility came after this fear. Ibn al-Qayyim explains the mention of hearing before seeing by the context of warning and by the central role of speech in human action.

This verse (20:47) reports that God commanded Moses and Aaron to go to Pharaoh, tell him they are messengers of his Lord, ask him to release the Children of Israel and not to torment them, and offer a sign from their Lord as proof. It adds that peace is for those who follow guidance. The commentators, from al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir to al-Baydawi, al-Nasafi and Ibn 'Ashur, agree that the torment consisted of forcing the Children of Israel into hard labour and killing their sons while sparing their women. The sign is generally identified as the staff and the white hand. All note that the singular 'sign' is used because the aim is to establish the claim to mission by its proof, not to count the miracles. On the phrase 'peace upon those who follow guidance', opinions differ: al-Zajjaj, Ibn Kathir and others take it not as a greeting but as a statement that whoever follows guidance is saved from God's punishment, while al-Zamakhshari links it to the angels guarding Paradise, and Ibn al-Qayyim sees it as a reassurance meant to encourage Pharaoh to accept the message. Al-Razi and Ibn Kathir treat the verse as evidence that the punishment of believers does not last. Ibn Kathir also reports Ibn 'Abbas describing it as the most hopeful verse for monotheists. The commentators do not settle between these readings, and the general sense of the mission remains an invitation supported by proof and gentleness.

The commentators place this verse within the message that Moses and Aaron are to deliver to Pharaoh: it has been revealed to them that punishment falls upon whoever denies and turns away. Al-Tabari and Qatada take denial to mean rejecting the Book of God and His obedience, while Ibn Kathir distinguishes denial of the heart from turning away in deed and supports this with other verses of warning. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and Abu Hayyan observe that the wording is deliberately indirect and does not name Pharaoh, which they regard as a wise way of warning. Ibn Abbas considers it among the most hopeful verses for monotheists, since they have neither denied nor turned away, and al-Nasafi understands the punishment as applying to unbelievers in general. Al-Razi argues from the definite article in 'the punishment' that it covers the whole category, so a believer who sins would not be punished forever, but al-Alusi replies that this inference fails if the article points to a specific punishment or if the sense is rhetorical. The commentators agree on the general meaning: a warning to those who deny and turn away, and an encouragement to follow guidance, through which peace is secured in this life and the next.

The Qur'an reports Pharaoh's question to Moses and Aaron after they had delivered their message: "Who then is your Lord, O Moses?" Moses alone is addressed because he is the principal in prophethood and Aaron his assistant; some commentators add that this matches the rhyme of the verses, others that Pharaoh, aware of a speech impediment in Moses' tongue, wanted to silence him, or that he wished to remind him of his upbringing in Pharaoh's household. Pharaoh's attribution of the Lord to the two messengers is read by several scholars as feigned ignorance. Moses' reply is accepted by all: their Lord is the One who gave every thing its creation and form and then guided it. The commentators differ on what this giving and guiding mean. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Suddi and Sa'id ibn Jubayr take it as giving each male its female of the same kind and guiding it to mating; Mujahid, 'Ata' and Muqatil take it as giving each thing its form and shape; al-Hasan and Qatada take it as giving each thing its welfare and guiding it to what sustains it; al-Dahhak applies it to the function of each limb, such as the hand for grasping and the eye for seeing. Al-Tabari favours a correspondence of form and kind between each creature and its mate, together with guidance to union, food and drink, while Ibn al-Qayyim holds that the guidance covers all of a creature's benefits. All see in the verse a proof that Pharaoh should acknowledge. Pharaoh then asks about the earlier generations, and Moses replies that their knowledge is with his Lord, in a Book that neither errs nor forgets; some note that Moses had no knowledge of them, since the Torah was revealed to him only after Pharaoh's death.

This passage records Moses' reply to Pharaoh, who had asked who their Lord is. Moses says that their Lord is the One who gave everything its creation, meaning its form and make suited to its purpose, and then guided it. The commentators agree that the verse offers evidence for the Creator from the perfection and guidance visible in creatures. They differ, however, on the precise meaning. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, al-Suddi and al-Farra' explain that it means giving each male its female of the same kind and guiding it to mate, al-Tabari presenting a closely related reading. Mujahid, 'Ata' and Muqatil take creation to mean form, al-Hasan and Qatada take it to mean what suits each thing and guides it to its welfare, and al-Dahhak understands it as the organs and their functions: the hand for grasping, the foot for walking, the eye for seeing. Al-Zamakhshari suggests that each thing is given what it needs and guided to use it, while Ibn 'Atiyya prefers the broader sense. According to Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi, Pharaoh, left without an answer, turned to the earlier generations, and Moses replied that their knowledge is with his Lord in a Book, where the Lord neither errs nor forgets. Al-Razi draws from the passage a rational argument for the existence of a Creator, and most commentators allow that these meanings can all be held together without choosing among them.

This passage of the story of Moses and Pharaoh follows Moses' answer about the Lord, who gave every thing its creation and then guided it. Pharaoh then asks about the earlier generations, who, in his view, did not worship God, such as the peoples of Noah, 'Ad and Thamud. The commentators agree that Moses entrusts the knowledge of them to God: it is recorded with my Lord in a Book, my Lord neither errs nor forgets, meaning that He does not mistake in His governance and misses nothing of their deeds, and will repay them for them. Al-Tabari and Mujahid hold that the two phrases mean the same thing, while most scholars distinguish between them: al-Qaffal takes the first as full knowledge and the second as its permanence, Ibn 'Abbas and al-Tabari understand error as a mistake in managing affairs, and Ibn al-A'rabi links the root to the idea of being absent. They differ on Pharaoh's purpose. Muqatil and others note that the Torah had not yet been revealed to Moses, so he had no knowledge of these stories. Others think Pharaoh aimed to challenge the claim of resurrection or the absence of worship among those peoples. Al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan see the question as evasion. Al-Razi reports that Moses set the topic aside and returned to proving God's oneness, while Ibn 'Ashur sees it as his refusal to be drawn into matters outside his mission.

The verse reports Moses's reply to Pharaoh, who asked about the fate of the earlier generations. The commentators explain that their knowledge is with his Lord, recorded in the Preserved Tablet; this belongs to the unseen, which only God knows, and Moses, as a servant, knows only what God has taught him. Most agree that "does not err" means God makes no mistake and nothing escapes Him, and that "does not forget" means He retains what He knows; al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir add that He does not err in His governance, while Ibn al-Jawzi reports from Mujahid that the two phrases have the same meaning. Al-Razi reports from al-Qaffal that the first refers to the breadth of divine knowledge and the second to its permanence. On the Book, al-Kalbi, al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir identify it as the Preserved Tablet, whereas al-Razi and al-Baydawi suggest the recording may be a figure of speech for the firmness of God's knowledge; al-Zamakhshari argues that divine knowledge cannot literally inhere in a written book. Opinions differ on why Pharaoh asked: al-Muqatil and Ibn al-Jawzi say he asked about past histories, others that he sought to divert Moses from his argument, al-Naqqash links the question to the warning of a believer from Pharaoh's household, and Ibn 'Ashur sees a tactic to embarrass Moses. All take the answer as an affirmation of God's comprehensive knowledge, and the commentators do not judge between these readings.

The commentators explain that this verse, part of Moses' words in reply to Pharaoh, describes God's blessings upon creation: He made the earth a cradle, a spread-out bed on which one rests and walks, He traced paths in it through mountains, valleys and deserts, and He sent down water from the sky by which He brings forth varied kinds of plants, differing in colour, taste and use. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Baydawi and Ibn Juzayy agree that it recalls God's favours and argues that the Creator who governs is the only Lord deserving worship. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and al-Qurtubi read it as a rational proof addressed to Pharaoh, who cannot claim any such power.

Readings differ on the word (mahdan). The Kufans read it with a fatha on the mim and a sukun on the ha, while the others read (mihadan) with a kasra and an alif. Abu Ubayd and Abu Hatim prefer the plural form, while others regard both as masdars or as nouns meaning a bed or couch. The exegetes treat both readings as valid and do not choose between them. On (shatta), al-Tabari and Ibn Abbas explain it as diverse, al-Qurtubi relates it to dispersal, and al-Zamakhshari allows it to qualify either the kinds or the plants.

The phrase (fa-akhrajna) is debated. Ibn Atiyya, al-Baydawi, Abu Hayyan and al-Zamakhshari see an iltifat, a shift from the third person to the first, signalling the majesty of the one who acts; others take it as Moses' own words, and al-Razi judges the first view the sounder. The commentators also explain that (ulu al-nuha) means those endowed with intellect, and that nuha is the reason that restrains its owner from vices. Finally, they note that (minha khalaqnakum) refers to the creation of Adam from earth, that return to the earth refers to death, and that being brought out refers to resurrection.

God tells people to eat from the fruits and plants He brings forth by rain, and to let their livestock graze on them, and He states that in this there are clear signs of His oneness for those who have understanding. Most commentators read the command as a permission and a favour: al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir address both people and their animals, while Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Qurtubi take it as a command of permission. On the phrase ulī al-nuhā, all agree it means people of reason, since nuhā denotes intellect because it restrains its owner from wrongdoing. Ad-Dahhak and Qatada add that these are those who refrain from what is forbidden, or who are pious, and Ibn Abbas glosses it as those with piety. There is a difference over who is speaking. Al-Razi, Ibn Atiyya and al-Baydawi connect the verse to Moses' argument with Pharaoh, whereas al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi, Abu Hayyan and al-Alusi take it as God's own words. Ibn Ashur treats it as a parenthetical remark within the story. The commentators explain that the pairs (azwaj) are varieties of plants, and that shatta means diverse in taste, colour and use, some suited to humans and others to animals. These works keep to this meaning and do not weigh between the views.

The commentators explain that this verse reminds people that God created them from the earth: their forefather Adam was formed from its dust, they are buried in it after death, and from it they will be brought out again on the Day of Resurrection. Most, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Nasafi, take the pronouns "minha" and "fiha" to refer to the earth mentioned just before, and read "taratan ukhra" as "another time", meaning a second bringing-forth like the first. Al-Zamakhshari explains that this bringing-out means reassembling the scattered parts mixed with dust and returning them to life. Al-Mawardi, al-Sam'ani and Ibn al-Jawzi understand the creation as that of Adam, while Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Baydawi hold that every person shares in that origin. A view transmitted from Ata al-Khurasani says an angel takes dust from the place where a person will be buried and scatters it on the drop of semen, so that the human is formed from both; al-Shinqiti rejects this, noting that the Qur'an places the drop after the dust, with an interval. Al-Razi links the earthly origin to the food from which semen comes, and mentions a tradition about burial; he also offers the punishment of the grave as a possible meaning, which most others consider weak. Overall the exegetes see the verse as part of Moses' argument against Pharaoh, grounding belief in a Creator and the possibility of resurrection in the evident earthly blessings.

This verse says that God showed Pharaoh all His signs, yet he denied them and refused. Most commentators take the signs to be the nine well-known miracles given to Moses: the staff, the white hand, the flood, the locusts, the lice, the frogs, the blood, the years of drought and the loss of crops, along with the lifting of the mountain. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baydawi note that the word "all" is not meant absolutely but refers to these known signs, and that the possessive form gives them honour. Al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir emphasise that Pharaoh saw the signs with his own eyes, so his denial was stubborn and arrogant, a point Ibn Kathir links to a verse in Surat al-Naml. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi explain that the denial came from his wrongdoing and pride. Al-Baghawi and al-Ta'labi report that Pharaoh claimed the signs were sorcery. Ibn 'Ashur sees the oath and the particle "qad" as expressing wonder at Pharaoh's obstinacy. Al-Razi and others note that the word for sign can also refer to proofs of God's oneness. The verb "aba" means refusing faith and obedience, though al-Mawardi also suggests it may mean refusing to accept the proof. Al-Razi, al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi discuss the possible meanings of the verb "to show" as seeing or knowing, and Ibn 'Ashur and al-Shinqiti favour the sense of visual seeing.

The Qur'an reports Pharaoh's words to Moses after the signs were shown to him: 'Have you come to drive us out of our land with your sorcery?' The commentators agree that 'our land' means Egypt or the homes of the people, and that Pharaoh wants to portray Moses' mission as a plot to seize power. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi, Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Atiyya note that Pharaoh calls the signs sorcery, aiming to expel the people and hand rule to Moses. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi see the sentence as a pretext and a sign of distress, since, they argue, no sorcerer could dispossess a king of his realm, so his fear is visible. Abu al-Su'ud and al-Alusi explain that the interrogative particle denies and denounces a claim held to be absurd, and that it serves to incite the people against Moses. Ibn 'Ashur adds that Pharaoh's use of the plural aims to rally his subjects. On the word 'sawan', the readers differ between a kasra and a damma, and the scholars treat both as acceptable variants. Mujahid and Qatada take it to mean an equitable place, while Ibn Zayd understands a flat, open place where everything can be seen.

This passage in the story of Moses tells how Pharaoh, after seeing all the signs and rejecting them out of arrogance, accused Moses of bringing sorcery to drive the people from their land. He then vowed to bring sorcery like it and asked for a fixed appointment, which neither side would break, at an open, even place where all could watch. The commentators agree that the 'even place' means a central spot equally distant from both sides, as al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi report from Mujahid and Qatada, while Ibn Zayd understands a flat open ground where nothing blocks the view, and al-Kalbi understands a place other than this one. The readings differ between damma, read by Ibn Amir, Asim and Hamza, and kasra, read by the others, and al-Tabari holds that both are dialects with the same meaning. Scholars also differ on the word 'appointment': al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and Ibn Atiyya treat it at length, with Ibn Atiyya and al-Razi arguing that only a promise can be broken, while al-Zamakhshari weighs several grammatical options. Moses set the day of adornment, a festival for the people according to Mujahid, Qatada and as-Suddi, the day of Ashura according to Ibn Abbas, or other days such as the Coptic new year or a market day according to other reports, with the people gathered in the morning light so that the proof is clearer and doubt is removed, as al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir state.

This verse records the appointment Moses sets with Pharaoh and his magicians for the decisive contest. The commentators explain that the day of adornment was a festival day for the Egyptians, when they dressed up and set aside their work, and that people were to be gathered in the morning so that all could witness the contest and the truth would be made manifest. They differ on which day this was: Ibn Abbas and Sa'id ibn Jubayr say it was the day of Ashura, Mujahid, Qatada, al-Suddi and Ibn Zayd say it was an annual feast day, Qatada and Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab say it was a market day, al-Dahhak says Saturday, and others mention Nowruz or the day the canal was opened. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn Atiyya and al-Razi discuss whether the word appointment refers to a time or a place: Moses answers with a time, which by implication fixes a known place, thus matching Pharaoh's request. They agree that the morning was chosen so that the crowd would be large, the light sufficient and nothing hidden. On the word suwa, Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Qatada and al-Suddi take it to mean equitable or midway between the two sides, while Ibn Zayd takes it to mean a level, open ground where everyone can see. The commentaries also record the variant readings of suwa and of the day's case endings, and the different readings of the verb for gathering, without settling the matter.

This verse describes Pharaoh turning away after the appointment was set: the commentators say he withdrew, or turned away from the truth Moses brought, and began preparing his schemes. Most of them, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Nasafi and Abu al-Su'ud, take the word kayd to mean magic and stratagem, and say that Pharaoh gathered the magicians from the cities of his realm before coming to the meeting on the day of adornment, in the morning. Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi report that there were seventy-two magicians or more, while others give much larger figures, as al-Qurtubi notes. Al-Razi points out that the verb tawalla can mean either opposing or leaving, and he prefers leaving the assembly here. Ibn 'Ashur sees the gathering as a deliberate preparation of the argument, whereas al-Sha'rawi reads the scheming as a sign of weakness. On the day of adornment, most take it to be a festival, though others name Ashura, the Persian New Year or a market day. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi also debate whether the word mawid refers to a time or a place, and both accept that it can imply both. The commentators agree in the end that Pharaoh came to the appointment after assembling his schemes.

This verse records Moses telling the magicians whom Pharaoh had gathered: woe to you, do not invent lies against God, lest He destroy you with a punishment, for whoever fabricates lies against God is ruined. The commentators report that his words moved them: they disputed among themselves and held a secret consultation. Qatada says they wondered whether, if he was a magician, they could defeat him, and if he came from heaven, the matter belonged to Him; al-Dahhak says they began to doubt that these were the words of a magician. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and most exegetes take the lie to be the claim that Moses' signs are mere sorcery, and the destruction to mean being wiped out. The readings differ: yasḥatakum with an open yā' is the Hijazi form, while yusḥitakum with a dammed yā' is the Najdi and Tamimi form; al-Tabari finds the first more eloquent, and Ibn Kathir treats both as equivalent. For the phrase 'these two are indeed magicians', Ibn Kathir and al-Zamakhshari cite the dialect of Kinana and Khath'am which keeps the dual with alif, and some explain the particle as meaning 'yes', while al-Farra' and others offer grammatical explanations; some reject the reading as contrary to the written text. Finally, 'the most excellent way' is understood by Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Zayd and others as the nobles and customs of the people, or by Qatada as the Children of Israel, though al-Tabari rejects Ibn Zayd's reading.

This passage describes what happened among the magicians after Moses had admonished them not to fabricate lies against God and warned them of His punishment. The plain meaning is that they disputed among themselves and conferred privately about how to face the contest. The commentators differ on what this dispute and secret conversation contained. Qatada and Ibn Abbas, as transmitted through Abu Ubayda and others, report that they said: if this is a sorcerer we will overcome him, and if it is from heaven then the matter is his; or, according to another report, that if Moses defeats us we will follow him. Ibn Ishaq, as-Suddi, Muqatil and ad-Dahhak hold that their secret talk was the statement: these two are indeed sorcerers who want to drive you out of your land with their magic. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi note that the open declaration was this statement, which they devised and arranged out of fear of being defeated and to discourage people from following them. On the reading of the words inna hadhani, the commentators offer several explanations: a dialect of the tribes of Bani al-Harith ibn Ka'b, Kinana and Khath'am; a reading in which inna means yes; an implied pronoun; or a copying error, as reported from Aisha and Abu Amr, a view that Ibn Taymiyya rejected. On the phrase your best way, Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and Qatada take it to mean your notables and people of wisdom, with Qatada identifying them as the Children of Israel, while Ibn Zayd takes it to mean your religion and custom; at-Tabari preferred the view of the exegetes over that of Ibn Zayd. Al-Mawardi and al-Zamakhshari note that the word way can denote the leaders of a people, and that al-muthla is the feminine of the superlative, meaning the best.

This passage reports what the magicians said after Moses had warned them not to invent lies against God. They then argued among themselves and whispered in private. The commentators broadly agree on the plain meaning: the magicians claimed that Moses and Aaron are two sorcerers who want, through their magic, to drive the people of Egypt from their land and to take away their best way of life. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Abbas explain that the best way refers to the notables and people of intellect, while Qatada took it to mean the Children of Israel, who were then the most numerous and wealthy. Al-Tabari also cites Ibn Zayd and al-Kisa'i, who understood it as the custom and religion the people follow, though he considers this a weaker reading than the majority view. Ibn Kathir and al-Baydawi note that these words were probably prompted by Pharaoh himself. On the content of the secret talk, Qatada reports the statement that if this is magic they will overcome it, al-Kalbi the vow to follow Moses if he prevails, and al-Zamakhshari a careful shaping of the words. On recitation, al-Tabari, al-Razi and al-Qurtubi record several readings of the words for 'indeed' and 'these two'. The majority reading is explained by grammarians either as a dialect in which the dual keeps its alif in every case, or as using 'inna' in the sense of 'yes'. Ibn 'Ashur rejects the report that the Qur'anic script contains an error. The commentators converge on the point that the magicians conferred to unite against Moses and then resolved to come forward in tight ranks to impress the onlookers.

This passage describes the confrontation between Moses and the magicians whom Pharaoh had gathered. After Moses warned them not to invent lies against God, lest they be destroyed, the magicians conferred among themselves in secret and agreed to say that Moses and Aaron were sorcerers who wanted to drive them from their land and take away their excellent way of life, meaning their rank and their notables. On the phrase "fa-ajmi'ū kaydakum", al-Tabari and the grammarians such as al-Farra' explain it as resolving firmly and agreeing without dispute. Abu 'Amr read "fa-jma'ū", meaning gather your sorcery together, but al-Tabari preferred the hamza reading because the readers agreed on it. For "thumma'tū ṣaffan", most exegetes take it as coming in close ranks, which is more awe-inspiring, while Abu 'Ubayda took it as the place of assembly or prayer ground, a reading al-Zamakhshari found plausible if that place was known. As for "qad aflaha al-yawma man ista'lā", most understand it as: whoever prevails has succeeded. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi treat it as a parenthetical remark, and al-Raghib leaves open that it may be God's words rather than the magicians'. Several commentators also report that these words may have come from Pharaoh himself.

This verse recounts how the magicians, after gathering their forces and lining up before Moses, courteously gave him the choice: he could throw his staff first, or they could be the first to throw theirs. The commentators explain that the particle "an" with its verb is either governed by an implied verb meaning "choose", or is the subject of an omitted statement, "the matter is your throwing or our throwing". Abu Hayyan prefers the implied reading "your throwing first". All agree that this offer reflected good manners toward Moses, who told them to throw first. The number of magicians differs widely among the reports. Al-Tabari, al-Qurtubi and al-Sudi speak of tens of thousands, some saying seventy thousand, while Ibn Jurayj gives nine hundred, Ibn Abbas seventy-two, and Ibn Kathir cites figures from twelve thousand to nineteen thousand. Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn Atiyya observe that these reports conflict. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and al-Zamakhshari relate that the ropes and staffs had been smeared with mercury, which, heated by the sun, made them move, so that Moses seemed to see them slithering like snakes. Ibn Atiyya holds that they really moved by trickery, while others say they did not move at all and only the onlookers' sight was deceived. Ibn Ashur adds that the illusion affected what Moses saw, not his own mind.

The verse describes Moses, who, when the magicians offered him the choice of throwing first or going after them, told them to throw first. They threw their ropes and staffs, and under their sorcery Moses imagined that they were slithering like snakes. The commentators agree that this was an illusion rather than a reality: al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Abu Hayyan report that the magicians had filled their ropes and staffs with mercury, which moved when heated by the sun. The number of magicians is widely disputed: seventy thousand according to al-Qasim ibn Abi Bazza, around thirty-four thousand according to al-Suddi, fifteen thousand according to Wahb ibn Munabbih, nine hundred according to Ibn Jurayj, and seventy-two according to Ibn Abbas. Al-Razi holds that the Quran does not settle the matter. As to why Moses let them throw first, most commentators explain that he wanted their entire magic to be displayed before his miracle annulled it, while Ibn Atiyya and al-Zamakhshari see it as a courteous exchange, and al-Zamakhshari believes God inspired it. Scholars also differ on the reading of 'yukhayyalu' (with a masculine or feminine verb), the feminine linking the effect to the ropes and staffs and the masculine to the sorcery; al-Tabari upholds the masculine reading as the common practice. Several commentators report that Moses felt fear, which some attribute to ordinary human nature and others to concern that the people might be misled.

The commentators explain that Moses felt a fear within himself when he saw the ropes and staffs of the magicians appear to move like snakes, and that God immediately reassured him and told him to cast down his staff. Most attribute this fear to human nature: al-Hasan, al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi describe a natural reaction to a frightening sight, and Abu al-Su'ud mentions the common human aversion to snakes. Muqatil, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir report instead that Moses feared people would be misled and would not believe, and Ibn al-Jawzi considers this the sounder view. Al-Tabari, al-Razi and Ibn Kathir explain that the magic produced the appearance of movement, some adding that the staffs had been coated with mercury which moved in the sunlight, while Abu Hayyan and al-Razi stress that the movement was only an illusion to the eye. On the phrase 'what is in your right hand', al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi note it may serve to belittle or to magnify the staff. On the sense of 'the magician does not prosper wherever he goes', most understand that he does not attain his aim, while Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn al-Jawzi also take it to mean he is not safe, and a hadith cited by Ibn Kathir treats it as a ruling to kill sorcerers. The recitations of 'kayda sahir' and 'kayda sihr' are discussed without a firm decision.

The commentators explain that God told Moses, when he sensed fear within himself at the sorcerers' magic, not to be afraid, for he would be the one who prevails. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi agree that al-a'la means victory, triumph and manifest supremacy, and that the prohibition of fear serves to strengthen Moses' heart. As for the cause of his fear, al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi attribute it to a natural human disposition that is hard to avoid, while al-Mawardi and al-Razi report that he feared people would be confused and not follow him. Al-Qurtubi also mentions his fear that people might be tested before he cast his staff. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn Atiyya and al-Biqa'i note that the phrase 'what is in your right hand', without naming the staff, may be meant to belittle it against the multitude of ropes and staffs, or to exalt it. Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi report that the staff swallowed what the sorcerers had produced, and that their trickery relied on mercury or visual illusion, according to accounts cited by Ibn Atiyya and al-Razi. Readers differ on the reading of 'kayd sahir' and 'kayd sihr'. Al-Tabari adopts the majority reading and considers the two readings close in meaning. Ibn Kathir and al-Tabari also report that 'the magician does not prosper wherever he comes' means he does not attain his goal, while some read it as an order to kill the magician wherever he is found, a point the commentators do not settle.

God commands Moses to throw the staff in his right hand, and it swallows what the magicians have made. The verse states that their work is only the trickery of a magician, and that a magician does not prosper wherever he goes. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report that the staff swallowed all the ropes and rods, which had been coated with quicksilver so that the sun made them seem to move; Ibn Kathir also describes the staff becoming a great serpent. Al-Razi and Ibn 'Atiyya hold that the ropes and rods moved through artifice, and Ibn Kathir adds that it was an illusion. Al-Zamakhshari explains that the vague phrase 'what is in your right hand' both belittles the magic and magnifies the staff. The readings differ between 'kayd sahir' and 'kayd sihr', and al-Tabari considers the two meanings close, while Ibn Juzayy and al-Nasafi note that the singular denotes the category of magician. On 'does not prosper', Ibn 'Abbas says he will not be happy, others that he will be killed wherever found; Ibn Kathir cites a hadith to this effect, but most commentators judge it weak, and the question of the magician's punishment remains debated. Faced with the miracle, the magicians fall prostrate and declare their faith in the Lord of Aaron and Moses.

This verse describes the moment when Pharaoh's magicians, after throwing down their ropes and staffs, see Moses's staff swallow everything they had made. Realising that this was not sorcery but a sign from God, they fall prostrate and say: we believe in the Lord of Aaron and Moses. The commentators note that Aaron is named first mainly to match the verse endings, though some add that Aaron was older, or that Pharaon, who had raised Moses, might otherwise be thought the intended Lord. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi report that their prostration was so sudden it seemed like a fall, and some transmit that they saw their places in Paradise while prostrate, a view al-Razi considers distant but possible. Ibn Kathir and others stress that their faith rested on their own expertise in magic, which let them recognise a true miracle. Pharaoh's rebuke, asking whether they believed before he gave permission, is read differently by the reciters, and the commentators explain it as a way of discrediting Moses. The number of magicians is strongly disputed, ranging from seventy thousand according to al-Qasim ibn Abi Bazza to a much smaller number according to others, and the commentators do not settle it.

Pharaoh turns on the magicians after they have believed, asking whether they believed in Moses before he gave them leave, and calling Moses their chief who taught them magic. He threatens to cut off their hands and feet on opposite sides and to crucify them on palm trunks, and he declares that they will learn whose punishment is harsher and more lasting, his or the Lord of Moses. The commentators agree on the plain meaning: the cutting is of the right hand with the left foot, and the crucifixion is on palm trunks, which Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi report as the first time Pharaoh carried out such a punishment. Al-Tabari also reports from Qatada and al-Suddi accounts of the magicians being killed after the threat. On the word aydina, al-Tabari, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Zamakhshari take it to mean Pharaoh and Moses, while al-Razi and al-Baydawi take it to mean the Lord of Moses. Al-Zamakhshari sees arrogance and mockery of Moses in the phrase, and Ibn Kathir reads it as Pharaoh's attempt to sow doubt among the people. On the reading of the interrogative and declarative forms, al-Nasafi and Ibn Juzayy record both, and the commentators do not settle between them. Al-Shinqiti holds that God preserved the magicians from the punishment, while al-Sha'rawi considers it more likely that Pharaoh carried out his threat.

The Quran recounts the response of the magicians when Pharaoh threatens them: they say they will not prefer him over the clear signs that have come to them or over the One who created them, and that he may decide as he wishes, for his authority reaches only this worldly life. The commentators, from al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir to al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi, agree that the point is steadfastness in faith and indifference to the threat. As for "and Him who brought us into being", al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and others read it as linked to the signs, while al-Razi and al-Nasafi also allow that it may be an oath; al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj cited both readings. Regarding "the clear signs", Ibn Abbas and Muqatil took them to be the hand and the staff, while al-Sam'ani and al-Baghawi understood them more broadly as proofs or certainty, and Abu Hayyan notes that the magicians saw them more clearly than others did.

The statement that Pharaoh's power extends only to this life is read by most as a fact limited to this world. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Qurtubi note that "this life" is a time expression in the accusative, and that one reading gives it a passive form. As for "we believe in our Lord that He may forgive us our sins and the magic you forced us to practise", Ibn Abbas, Ibn Zayd and Ibn Kathir explain that Pharaoh compelled young men to learn sorcery, while al-Hasan held that they learned it as children and then practised it willingly, and al-Razi offered several possible explanations. Finally, "God is better and more enduring" is taken by most as a reply to Pharaoh's threat: God's reward is better and His punishment more lasting. The commentators do not decide between these views.

This verse records the magicians' reply to Pharaoh, who had threatened to cut off their hands and feet and crucify them after they believed in Moses. They say they will not prefer him to the clear proofs that have come to them or to the One who created them, and that his power extends only to this worldly life. They then declare their faith in the Lord of Moses and Aaron, asking Him to forgive their sins and the magic he compelled them to perform. The commentators agree that the sins refer to disbelief and wrongdoing. They differ on the nature of the compulsion. Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Zayd say Pharaoh took boys from the Children of Israel and had them taught magic, al-Baghawi and Muqatil say most of the magicians were Israelites whom Pharaoh forced to learn it, and al-Hasan says they were trained as children and afterwards practised it by choice. Al-Razi and Ibn al-Anbari understand the compulsion as being forced to confront Moses. Ibn Kathir reports that Pharaoh compelled them to gather and compete with Moses, and some hold that a ruler's command alone counts as compulsion. On the closing phrase, al-Tabari, Ibn Ishaq and al-Qurtubi explain that God's reward is better and His punishment more lasting, while Muhammad ibn Ka'b reads it as a direct reply to Pharaoh's threat, God being better in reward for those who obey Him and more lasting in punishment for those who disobey. Some exegetes accept that Pharaoh carried out his threat, while others refrain from deciding since no authentic report confirms it. All stress the firmness of the magicians' faith.

This verse, within the account of the magicians facing Pharaoh, states that whoever comes before his Lord as a criminal, meaning a disbeliever or one steeped in sin, will have Hell, where he will neither die to find rest nor live a life that benefits him. The commentators differ on who is speaking. Al-Tabari, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Qurtubi take the words to be the magicians' admonition to Pharaoh, while others, such as al-Baghawi and al-Baydawi, present it as a statement from God, and some note that either reading is possible. Most agree that the 'criminal' here is the disbeliever, though al-Qurtubi also allows that it may refer to one who persists in sins. Ibn Kathir cites a hadith from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri distinguishing the people of the Fire, who neither die nor live there, from sinful believers who will be brought out through intercession. Ibn 'Ashur explains that the life that is denied is one free of torment, since the punishment is continuous. Al-Razi gives an extended discussion of grave sins, reports the Mu'tazili argument drawn from this verse, answers their objections from his own school's standpoint, and concludes that the highest ranks belong to those who have purified themselves. The second part describes the highest ranks as the Gardens of Eden, with rivers flowing beneath, where one dwells forever. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that this reward is for one who has purified himself from disbelief and sin.

This part of the verse states that whoever comes to his Lord on the Day of Resurrection as a believer who has done righteous deeds will receive the high ranks, which the commentators understand as the lofty dwellings of Paradise. Ibn 'Abbas explains righteous deeds as the performance of the obligations, a view repeated by as-Sam'ani, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Baghawi. Al-Tabari, followed by Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi, holds that the high ranks are the Gardens of Eden through which rivers flow, the gardens being an explanation or apposition, while az-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and an-Nasafi treat them only as an apposition or further clarification. Ibn 'Ashur notes that these verses sit between the story of the magicians and the account of the Children of Israel's departure, serving as an admonition to the believers among Pharaoh's people. As for who speaks them, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Qurtubi report that one group considers them the words of the magicians addressed to Pharaoh, while another holds they are God's own address to the Prophet ﷺ. Most commentators understand the purification mentioned in 'whoever purifies himself' as cleansing from polytheism and sins, and al-Kalbi links it to the declaration that there is no god but God. Ar-Razi uses the verse in the debate over the threat of punishment, setting out the Mu'tazilite objections and their answers without settling the question.

This verse describes the reward of those who come to their Lord as believers who have done righteous deeds: gardens of Eden, that is, gardens of lasting abode, beneath which rivers flow, where they remain forever. The commentators explain that this reward is the high degrees promised to those who believe and act righteously. The phrase "whoever purifies himself" means, according to al-Tabari, al-Baghawi, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi, one who has purified himself from disbelief and sins, while Ibn 'Abbas and al-Kalbi add that it refers to uttering the declaration that there is no god but God. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir understand Eden as a lasting dwelling without departure or end. Al-Sam'ani cites a report attributed to 'Umar describing a palace of Eden with ten thousand doors, but no other major exegete adopts it. Grammarians differ: al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and Abu al-Su'ud treat "gardens of Eden" as an apposition to the degrees, whereas al-Tabari connects them to those degrees as a clarification. As to the speaker, al-Baghawi, al-Baydawi and al-Qurtubi report that these words are the magicians' admonition to Pharaoh, while Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Nasafi allow that they are God's own speech, a view al-Nasafi considers more apparent. Ibn 'Ashur sees them as an interjected passage between the story of the magicians and the Exodus narrative.

In this verse God says that He revealed to Moses that he should travel by night with His servants, the Children of Israel, out of Egypt, and strike for them a dry path through the sea, with no water or mud, assuring them that they would fear neither being overtaken by Pharaoh from behind nor drowning ahead of them. The commentators note that this command came after a long confrontation in which Pharaoh repeatedly broke his promises. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi agree that « yabasan » means dry, and that the prohibition of fear covers both Pharaoh and the sea. Al-Tabari reads « fadrib » as making or laying out a path, and al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi follow him, while al-Razi offers two meanings: making the path, or showing it by striking the sea with the staff. On the recitation « lā takhaf » with the jussive in Hamza's reading, al-Farra' and al-Tabari explain it as a response to the command or as a new prohibition, though al-Tabari prefers the indicative form for its eloquence. As to the number of paths opened, al-Razi, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Juzayy speak of twelve, one for each tribe, while others keep to the singular. The story's conclusion in the commentaries is the drowning of Pharaoh and his army, described in varying detail; al-Shinqiti refers to other surahs for the fuller account.

The commentators explain that God commanded Moses to travel by night with the Children of Israel and to open for them a dry path through the sea, so that they would fear neither being overtaken by Pharaoh nor drowning. When the Israelites entered the path, Pharaoh pursued them with his armies, and the sea closed over them all. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi agree that Pharaoh misled his people and did not guide them, meaning that he led them to destruction instead of setting them on a right course, which contradicts his claim to show them only the way of right guidance. According to Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi, the phrase 'what covered them' refers to a well-known event whose horror cannot be described. Al-Zamakhshari sees a concise expression that conveys many meanings, and holds that the repetition increases the sense of dread. Al-Tabari stresses that Pharaoh had ordered his people not to follow Moses.

The scholars differ on the shape of the path. Ibn Atiyya, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir hold that the sea split into twelve paths, one for each tribe, citing the verse 'each part was like a great mountain.' Al-Razi notes that the wording may also refer to a single path, and that the reports mention several. Al-Razi also records the account that Gabriel rode a mare that drew Pharaoh's horse into the water, but he finds this explanation unlikely.

On recitation, Hamza reads 'la takhaf' in the jussive, as a response to the command or as a prohibition, while most readers use the indicative 'la takhafu'. Al-Farra and al-Zajjaj accept both readings. In the following verses, readers differ over 'fayahilla' and 'fayahulla', and al-Farra prefers the kasra form, meaning 'be due', rather than 'descend'.

The commentators explain that Pharaoh led his people astray from the right path by calling them to disbelief and to denying Moses, and that he did not guide them to safety but brought them to ruin. The verse thus answers Pharaoh's own claim, "I only show you the way of right guidance." Most exegetes see it as the conclusion of the account of Moses and the Children of Israel being saved and Pharaoh and his armies drowning, describing the end of misguidance. Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi read "nor did he guide" as meaning he did not lead them to the right way; al-Baydawi, Abu al-Su'ud and al-Alusi see a scope that is both religious and worldly, the ruin reaching this life as well as the next. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and al-Qurtubi take "nor did he guide" as a mocking reference to Pharaoh or as an emphasis on misguidance, since one who misleads may guide no one, or may guide in some matters. Al-Razi and the Mu'tazili Qadi 'Abd al-Jabbar use the verse in the debate over whether God creates human actions; al-Razi answers by denying that the principle is universal, though that debate goes beyond the verse's plain sense. Commentary on the details of the drowning and the rescue draws largely on narratives from Jewish and Christian sources or on traditions outside the verse itself. Modern commentators stress mainly that disbelief and straying lead to destruction, and that Pharaoh was lying when he claimed to guide his people.

This verse reminds the Children of Israel of God's favours: He rescued them from their enemy Pharaoh, appointed a meeting for them at the right side of Mount Tur where the Torah would be given, and sent down manna and quails as food in the wilderness. Most commentators understand the address to be to the Children of Israel of Moses's time, while al-Baydawi and Abu al-Su'ud allow that it may also address Jews in the Prophet's time, reminded of what was done for their forefathers. Ibn Kathir and others describe the manna as a sweet substance falling from heaven and the quails as a bird like the quail of the Mediterranean, while al-Jaza'iri describes the manna as something white like snow. The commentators agree that the command to eat is a permission rather than an obligation, and that the prohibition of transgression covers wronging one another, ungratefulness for the blessing, extravagance, using the provision for disobedience, and storing it beyond the needs of a day and a night, as Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid report. As for the phrase 'then My anger descends upon you', it is read with a kasra on the first letter, meaning it becomes due, or with a damma, meaning it descends. Al-Tabari judges both readings correct, since the two meanings are close. Most explain 'hawa' as perishing and falling into the Fire. The verse closes with the promise of forgiveness for whoever repents, believes and does righteous deeds. The meaning of 'then he was guided' varies: Ibn Kathir and most others take it as steadfastness in Islam until death, others as knowing that the deed earns reward, and Ibn 'Atiyya prefers guarding one's beliefs from any error.

God tells the Children of Israel to eat of the good things He has provided, and warns them against transgressing in them, for whoever is struck by His anger is ruined and falls. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi explain that transgression means failing to give thanks or misusing these gifts through waste and sin. Al-Mawardi also includes hoarding beyond a day and night, and using provision to disobey God, reporting from Ibn Abbas that food spoils when stored. Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Nasafi add that transgression may mean wronging one another, while al-Zamakhshari lists denying the blessing, spending it on sin, withholding the poor's rights, and arrogance. The commentators agree that the good things are what is lawful and pleasant, though al-Razi and al-Qurtubi take the manna and quails as examples of pleasant food, while al-Kalbi and Muqatil simply say lawful. The verb yahilla may be read with a kasra, meaning it becomes due, or with a damma, meaning it descends; al-Qurtubi prefers the kasra. Most read hawa as ruin, and al-Mawardi and al-Zamakhshari relate it to falling into the fire. All agree that God forgives those who repent, believe and do good. On the phrase thumma ihtada, Ibn Abbas takes it as not doubting one's faith, Qatada and Ibn Kathir as holding to Islam until death, Ibn Atiyya and al-Razi as steadfastness, al-Mawardi and Ibn Sa'di as following the Sunna, and Thabit al-Bunani as loyalty to the family of the Prophet. Al-Tabari favours remaining steadfast in guidance.

This verse states that God is very forgiving toward those who turn back from polytheism and sin, believe, do righteous deeds, and then stay on the right path. The commentators broadly agree on the basic meaning: repentance begins with abandoning association with God, followed by faith and good works. The phrase "then guided" is explained in several ways. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi favour the view that it means remaining steadfast in faith until death, a view also reported from Qatada and al-Thawri. Ibn Abbas says it means not doubting one's faith, Sa'id ibn Jubayr says it means holding firmly to the Sunna and the community, al-Rabi' ibn Anas says it means following the Prophet's example, and Ibn Zayd says it means doing the deed correctly. Al-Kalbi, al-Sha'bi and Muqatil say it means knowing that there is a reward for one's actions. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Ashur note that "then" marks a higher rank, that of steadfastness, which is greater than merely beginning to do good. Al-Razi offers three readings: continuing on the path, recognising that guidance comes from God, or purifying the heart of blameworthy traits. Al-Thaalabi and al-Baydawi also report the view, attributed to Thabit al-Bunani, that it refers to loyalty to the family of the Prophet. Ibn Kathir adds that God accepted the repentance even of those who had worshipped the calf.

God asks Moses, peace be upon him, why he rushed ahead of his people, a question that carries both rebuke and disapproval. The commentators agree that Moses went ahead out of longing for the speech of his Lord and a desire for His pleasure, and he answered that his people were close behind him and that he hurried to his Lord so that He would be pleased. They differ on who the 'people' were: al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi understand the seventy men chosen for the appointment, whereas al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan understand the tribal chiefs (nuqaba'), and others take in all the Israelites left with Harun. They also differ on the grounds of the rebuke: some see haste itself as a flaw, others see the fault in leaving the people behind without bringing them along. Al-Baydawi explains that Moses answered the more important point, the abandonment, first. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi hold that Moses erred in his judgement and deserved reproach, while Ibn 'Atiyya sees an interpretive effort driven by the wish to draw near to God. Ibn al-Qayyim draws from the verse the recommendation to hasten to acts of obedience, citing Ibn Taymiyya on praying at the start of the prayer time. Ibn 'Ashur notes that Moses left his people before God had instructed him to guard them against deception. Differences in recitation, such as the madd or qasr in ulaa and the fatha or kasra in athari, do not alter the essential meaning. In short, the verse combines a reproach for haste with an expression of sincere love and longing for God.

The verse recounts the exchange between God and Moses when Moses had gone ahead of his people to meet his Lord at Mount Sinai. God asks what made him hasten away from his people, and Moses replies that they are close behind him and that he hurried toward his Lord to win His good pleasure. Most commentators, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi, take the people to be the seventy chosen men who were to accompany him, while Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn al-Jawzi understand the whole of the Children of Israel left under Aaron. On the phrase 'upon my footsteps', some say they are near and will catch up with him, while others say they were waiting for his return. On 'that You may be pleased', al-Tabari, Ibn Zayd and al-Baghawi explain it as a wish for increased pleasure, Qatada as longing, and al-Daqqaq as Moses concealing his longing behind the word 'pleasure'. Ibn al-Qayyim reports that Ibn Taymiyya drew from the verse the preference for praying at the start of the prayer time. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi discuss the form of God's question and the rebuke it implies. Al-Zamakhshari holds that Moses erred in his reasoning and deserved reproach, whereas al-Baydawi, al-Nasafi and Abu al-Su'ud present his action as a praiseworthy effort of judgement. Ibn 'Ashur notes that God rebukes him for overlooking the consequences of leaving his people early, namely the temptation that followed.

God tells Moses that his people were tested with the worship of the calf after he left them, and that the Samiri led them astray by calling them to worship it. The commentators agree that the 'trial' refers to the actual sin the Israelites committed, and that the Samiri was the direct cause of their misguidance. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi link the fitna to the real worship of the calf. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi also give the sense of a test, al-Razi explaining that it may be an increase in religious obligations. The reading 'wa adallu-hum' with a nominative, noted by al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan, makes the Samiri the most misguided of them. On his identity, al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir place him among the Israelites or the tribe of Samira, while al-Mawardi and others mention that he was from Kerman or a Copt, as reported by Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Zamakhshari and Ibn al-Jawzi. Several authors say the calf was cast from the jewellery borrowed from the Egyptians. As to its lowing, al-Razi and Ibn Kathir note that some held it to be truly alive, while others said it was only the wind entering its hollow body. The commentators report these views without judging between them.

This verse describes Moses returning to his people angry and grieved after his encounter with his Lord, and rebuking them: did your Lord not make you a good promise? The commentators differ on what this promise was. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi take it to be the gift of the Torah, containing guidance and light, and Ibn Kathir extends it to the blessings that follow reaching Mount Sinai. Al-Mawardi, al-Razi and Ibn al-Jawzi also mention victory, reward for good deeds, or the promise of forgiveness for whoever repents, believes and acts righteously. As for the question of whether a long time has passed, al-Tabari, Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn Kathir read it as referring to the length of Moses' absence, and so to forgetfulness, while al-Zamakhshari and al-Alusi understand it as the period of separation, and al-Sa'di suggests it may refer to a long interval since prophecy. On the meaning of asif, most follow Ibn Abbas, Qatada and Mujahid in understanding sorrow, whereas al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and Ibn Kathir stress extreme anger, and al-Razi combines the two. The people's excuse, that they did not break the promise by their own power, is reported by many commentators, along with the jewellery borrowed from the Copts, which some regard as a sinful burden, and the calf made by al-Samiri. The verse closes by pointing out that the calf neither speaks nor can harm or benefit. In short, the verse is a rebuke for breaking a covenant, and the commentators mainly debate the meaning of the promise and the nature of Moses' distress.

The commentators explain that when Moses returned to his people, angry and grieved, he reminded them of their Lord's good promise of the Torah and of victory. The Children of Israel replied that they had not broken their pledge by their own choice, but had been burdened with loads of the jewelry of Pharaoh's people, which they threw away, and that the Samiri likewise threw what he had. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir note that the word « bi-mulkina » is read in three ways, and most exegetes see these readings as close in meaning: by our command, by our strength, or, according to Ibn Zayd, because we did not control ourselves. As for the « burdens », Mujahid and al-Suddi understand them as loads of jewelry, while others take them to mean sins, since such spoils were not lawful for them at that time. Al-Mawardi and al-Razi record the views on « he forgot »: Ibn Abbas and Mujahid say Moses forgot his Lord and went to seek Him elsewhere, while others say the Samiri abandoned his faith. Regarding the calf's lowing, some hold that it was truly alive, while Mujahid and others say the sound came from wind passing through openings in it. Al-Razi also reports the theological debate between the Mu'tazilites and the Sunni scholars over who caused the misguidance, and the text does not settle it.

This passage describes how, during Moses' absence, the Samiri fashioned for the Israelites a calf with a body and a lowing sound from the ornaments they had borrowed from Pharaoh's people, and how those who were led astray said: this is your god and the god of Moses, whom he has forgotten. The commentators agree that the calf was made from the borrowed ornaments. They differ on how it produced its sound: Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan and Qatada hold that it was truly alive and lowed, while Mujahid, followed by al-Razi and Ibn Kathir, holds that the sound came from wind passing through openings in the figure. Al-Zamakhshari and others also mention the view that dust from the hoof of Gabriel's mount gave it life. The word "fa-nasiya" has several readings: al-Tabari, Qatada and al-Suddi take it as Moses having lost track of his god, while Ibn Zayd and another report of Ibn 'Abbas take it as the words of the Samiri or as God's statement about him, the Samiri having abandoned his faith. On the phrase "bi-malkina", Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid say by our command, Qatada and al-Suddi say by our strength, and Ibn Zayd says by our own passion overcoming us; al-Tabari judges these meanings to be close. The three vowel readings are regarded by most as equivalent. The closing argument, noted by most exegetes, shows the absurdity of the worship: the calf cannot answer them or bring them harm or benefit.

God challenges those who worshipped the calf: do they not see that this calf, which they claim as a god, does not answer them when they speak and has no power to harm or to benefit them? How could one with such qualities be a god? The commentators agree that the calf is the one fashioned by al-Samiri during Moses' absence, and that the rebuke is addressed to the Children of Israel and their leaders. They differ on the lowing of the calf: Ibn Abbas and others say it was a real voice given to it by God, while Mujahid holds that the sound came from the wind entering its hollow body, with no life in it. Al-Tabari and others report that Aaron had warned them and asked them to follow him, but they insisted on clinging to the calf until Moses returned. On the word 'forgot' in the preceding verse, Ibn Kathir reports that some take it to refer to Moses, who had forgotten to tell them the calf was not their god, while others take it to refer to al-Samiri, who abandoned his faith. Readings such as 'yarji'u', 'mulkina' and 'humilna' are discussed by grammarians and reciters, and the commentators do not settle between them.

This verse reports that Harun warned his people before Musa returned: the calf is only a trial that tested them, their Lord is the Most Merciful, and he commanded them to follow him and obey his command by abandoning the worship of the calf. They answered that they would remain devoted to the calf until Musa came back. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Nasafi read « before » as before Musa's return, whereas al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and Abu al-Su'ud take it as before Samiri spoke, so that Harun hurried to warn them as soon as they saw the calf. For al-Tabari and al-Sudi, the fitna is the trial they underwent through the calf; al-Mawardi and al-Qurtubi add that Harun withdrew with twelve thousand men who had not worshipped it. On « follow me », Ibn Abbas and Ibn al-Jawzi understand it as walking with him and separating from the rest, Ibn Atiyya links it to the journey to Mount Sinai, and most commentators take it to mean holding firm to the religion. Al-Razi sees the order of the address as deliberate: remove falsehood, know God, follow the prophet, then observe the law. Ibn Kathir reports that the people opposed Harun and nearly killed him. Ibn Ashur notes that this passage contradicts the Jewish books' claim that Harun made the calf.

This verse reports the reply of the Children of Israel when Harun (Aaron), peace be upon him, advised them after they had been led astray by the calf made by al-Samiri. He had warned them that the calf was a trial, that their Lord was the Most Merciful, and he had commanded them to follow and obey him. They answered that they would remain devoted to the calf until Musa returned. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi explain that 'akifin' means remaining steadfastly in worship, and the commentators agree that this answer shows their stubbornness in error. Ibn Kathir adds that they opposed Harun and nearly killed him. Al-Mawardi and al-Nasafi report that he withdrew from them with twelve thousand who had not worshipped the calf. On the meaning of 'until Musa returns', al-Tabari and al-Nasafi take it that they wanted to see whether Musa too would worship the calf, while al-Alusi suggests they had in fact resolved to follow him in this worship.
