Al-Razi sees in it the attitude of a blind follower who prefers Musa's word to the clear proof Harun presented. Az-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan note that 'lan' does not necessarily imply permanence, since it is followed by 'hatta'. Ibn 'Ashur highlights the logical order of Harun's address, moving from the warning against a false god to the call to recognise the true Lord, and then to follow the prophet.

The Quran recounts Moses' rebuke of his brother Harun on his return from Mount Sinai to find his people worshipping the calf: what prevented you, when you saw them going astray, from following me? Did you disobey my command to take my place among my people, to reform and not follow the way of the corrupters? The commentators agree that Moses seized his brother's beard and head in anger, but they differ on the meaning of 'not following me'. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Tabari and Ibn al-Jawzi take it to mean leaving the people and following Moses with the believers, al-Mawardi gives the sense of not following him in rejecting idolatry, and Ibn 'Atiyya suggests not walking with him toward Mount Tur. Mujahid and al-Zamakhshari read it as a call to zeal for God and to fight the unbelievers, while al-Razi and Ibn 'Ashur explore more nuanced readings of policy and prudence. On the particle 'la', most exegetes regard it as superfluous, while the grammarians see it as an emphatic negation. Al-Razi lists three possible motives for Moses' gesture, and Ibn Kathir stresses that Harun was respectful and obedient. Harun's answer, that he feared Moses would accuse him of dividing the children of Israel, is explained by al-Tabari as fear that the people would split or fight, and he is said not to have kept his brother's word.

The verse records Moses rebuking his brother Harun after his return from Mount Sinai and finding the people worshipping the calf. He asks what prevented him, when he saw them going astray, from following him, and whether he disobeyed his command. Most commentators treat the particle la as an emphatic addition, so the sentence is a rebuke and a reproach. They differ on what 'following' meant. Ibn 'Abbas, as transmitted by al-Tabari, Ibn Jurayj and Ibn Kathir, understood it as leaving with those who remained faithful. Muqatil, and Ibn al-Jawzi in one view, read it as confronting and fighting them, while al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi spoke of zeal for God and fighting unbelief. Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan also allowed that it meant going up the mountain or carrying out reform. The command Harun disobeyed was Moses' charge to take his place among the people and set things right, which al-Shinqiti cites as evidence that a command implies obligation. Al-Tabari judged Ibn 'Abbas's reading the most sound. Harun answered that he feared Moses would say he had divided the Children of Israel, and the commentators report that he kept with him those who had not worshipped the calf.

This passage recounts Moses returning from Mount Sinai and rebuking his brother Harun for not following him when he saw the people going astray by worshipping the calf. In anger Moses seized his brother's beard and head, and Harun replied: "O son of my mother, do not seize my beard or my head; I feared that you would say, 'You have divided the Children of Israel and did not heed my word.'" The commentators agree on the general sense: Harun feared that leaving the people to join Moses would split them apart, and Moses blames him for not keeping his charge to put things right and not follow the way of the corrupters. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, following Ibn Jurayj, understood this charge as preserving the believers through patience and gentleness, with al-Tabari preferring Ibn Abbas's reading that Moses reproached him for not having followed him with the believers. Ibn Zayd took "following" to mean leaving with those who obeyed, while al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi read it as fighting against idolatry, and Muqatil as openly denouncing it. Several, including al-Qurtubi and al-Baydawi, add that Harun feared armed fighting among the Israelites. Al-Razi examined at length the objections concerning the infallibility of prophets raised by this incident, and several scholars, including al-Qurtubi and Ibn Ashur, explain that Moses acted out of anger rather than contempt. Ibn Ashur, however, judged Harun's choice to preserve the community's unity to be less weighty than preserving the faith itself.

Moses asks the Samiri about his affair and what moved him to act, namely to make the calf and worship it. The commentators agree that the word khatb refers to a grave matter, though they differ on how harsh the rebuke is. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Qurtubi take the Messenger to be Gabriel: the Samiri saw the hoofprint of his horse, took a handful of its dust and threw it onto the melted ornaments, which became a calf that lowed. They report that he recognised Gabriel because his mother had hidden him in a cave where the angel fed him. Al-Zamakhshari, Abu Hayyan and Ibn Ashur, followed by Abu Muslim al-Isfahani, hold instead that the Messenger is Moses himself and that the trace is his law and practice, an interpretation Ibn Ashur presents as figurative and less tied to Israelite narratives. On the readings, transmitters differ between baṣurtu with ya and tabṣurū with ta, and between qabḍa with the emphatic dad and qabṣa with sad, the first meaning a grip with the whole palm and the second with the fingertips. Opinions also vary on the Samiri's identity: some name his tribe or village of Samira, others Kirman or Bajarma, and some doubt that he was of the Children of Israel. Many report that Moses banished him and forbade people to touch him, so that he would say: no touching.

The verse records the Samiri's answer when Moses asks what led him to make the calf. He says he saw what the others did not see, namely Gabriel on a horse, and took a handful from the trace of the horse's hoof and threw it onto the molten gold, which became a calf that lowed. He adds that his own soul made this seem good to him. Most commentators identify the Messenger as Gabriel and the handful as the dust left by his horse. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi report from Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and Qatada that the Samiri saw Gabriel on the day the sea was parted or when Moses went up to Mount Sinai, and from Ibn Juraij and al-Suddi the story of his infancy in a cave where Gabriel nursed him, which explains why he recognised him. Al-Razi, al-Shawkani and al-Qasimi present, without making it the majority view, the opinion of Abu Muslim al-Isfahani that the Messenger is Moses and his trace is his law and practice, which the Samiri rejected. Ibn Ashur judges that the stories about Gabriel appear neither in the Israelite texts nor in the Sunnah. The readings differ: Hamza and al-Kisa'i read the verb in the second person, and al-Hasan and Qatada read the noun with a sad. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn Atiyya and Abu Hayyan explain that qabda is a grip with the whole hand and qabsa a grip with the fingertips. All agree that Moses banished the Samiri and ordered the people to shun him, but they differ on the meaning of 'la misas': a prohibition on touching for fear of fever, according to Qatada; social isolation, according to Abu Hayyan; or a sense linked to childlessness, according to Abu Muslim.

This verse records Moses' words to the Samiri after he had confessed to making the calf: go away, and your penalty in this life will be to say all your days, « No touching », that is, do not touch me and I will not touch you, since whoever touched him or was touched by him was seized with fever, so he lived apart and people kept their distance from him. As for his punishment in the Hereafter, it is a promise that will not be broken, a reading that can also mean he cannot escape it or be spared it. Moses then tells him to look at his god, to which he remained devoted, and vows to burn it and then scatter its ashes into the sea. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and al-Baydawi agree that the punishment was social exile and that the calf was destroyed and scattered in the water. They differ on how it was destroyed: al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir take burning as the meaning, while Abu Ja'far the reciter, Ibn Abbas and Ali, as reported by Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Razi, read it as filing it down with a file; al-Suddi, cited by Ibn al-Jawzi, Abu Hayyan and al-Razi, combines slaughter, filing and burning. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi also discuss the meaning of touching, which Abu Muslim, as reported by al-Razi, links to the cutting off of offspring. The passage closes with the commentators' affirmation that God alone is the true god, whose knowledge encompasses all things.

This verse states that the only true God for the Children of Israel is Allah, and there is no god but Him. It comes in the story of the Samiri, after he made the calf that the people worshipped. Most commentators understand these words to be Moses' own, and their meaning is that His knowledge encompasses everything, nothing escapes Him. This is the view of al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Nasafi, al-Baydawi and al-Qasimi, among others. All agree that the calf cannot be a deity, since it knows nothing and can do nothing.

On the grammar of the final word, "ilman", most commentators read it as a tamyiz, a specifying accusative that stands for the subject: His knowledge encompassed every thing. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn Atiyya and Abu Hayyan support this. A reading attributed to Mujahid and Qatada, with the sin doubled, makes "ilman" the direct object instead. Al-Razi regards the phrase as among the most eloquent in the Qur'an. For Ibn Ashur, the verse teaches the community the attributes of the true God, and His oneness includes all His attributes; universal knowledge invites believers to be mindful of Him in private and in public.

Ibn Sa'di links the phrase to God's perfection, the One who has the most beautiful names and the highest attributes and who alone deserves worship. The commentators do not disagree about the basic meaning of the verse; their differences concern mainly grammar and recitation.

God tells His Prophet ﷺ that just as He has related to him the story of Moses, Pharaoh and the Children of Israel, He will relate to him the accounts of earlier nations, and that He has given him from His presence the Qur'an as a reminder (dhikr). The commentators agree that the dhikr here is the Qur'an, as al-Tabari, al-Baghawi, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi report. They also agree that whoever turns away from it, neither believing in it nor acting upon it, will carry a burden (wizr) on the Day of Resurrection, meaning a sin and a heavy punishment, in which he will abide forever, and that this burden is an evil one to bear. Al-Tabari and Mujahid take wizr to mean sin, while al-Zamakhshari reads it as a heavy punishment, called a burden by analogy with what weighs down the one who carries it. Al-Zamakhshari also notes that the subject of the verb 'sa'a' is implicit and is explained by the word 'burden'. Ibn 'Ashur sees the verse as a closing summary that returns to the story of Moses. Al-Shinqiti considers the passage proof of the Prophet's truthfulness, since he was unlettered and could only have known these accounts through revelation. Ibn Kathir stresses that the warning applies to everyone who has received the Qur'an, Arab or not. The scholars differ on the sense of 'min' in 'min anba'', which many take as partitive, meaning the Prophet is told only some of these accounts.

This passage tells us that God recounts to His Prophet ﷺ the stories of past nations, as He recounted the story of Moses and Pharaoh, and that He gave him the Quran as a reminder and admonition. The commentators explain that whoever turns away from this reminder, meaning does not believe in it or act upon it, will carry on the Day of Resurrection a burden, wizr. Al-Tabari and Mujahid take this to mean sin, while al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and al-Baydawi explain that the word denotes a heavy punishment, likened to a load that weighs down the one who carries it. Ibn Kathir holds that this warning applies to everyone who has received the Quran, whether Arab, non-Arab or People of the Book. The exegetes agree that "abiding therein" means remaining in the recompense of this burden, which al-Qurtubi identifies as Hell. They differ on the sense of "sa'a": al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi take it in the sense of "bi'sa" with an implied object, while others make the subject a pronoun referring to the burden. The following verses describe the terrors of the Last Day and the blast of the trumpet. Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada and al-Zuhri give several meanings to "zurqan": blue or blinded eyes according to some, pallid complexions or severe thirst according to others. As for the duration of the stay mentioned, opinions differ: between the two blasts according to some, the length of worldly life or the stay in the grave according to others.

The commentators explain that this verse describes the fate of one who turns away from the Qur'an, neither believing in it nor acting upon it: on the Day of Resurrection he will carry a heavy burden, namely a sin or a grievous punishment, and he will remain in it forever, and how evil is the burden they have taken upon themselves. They agree that the burden refers to the weight of the punishment or the sin that brought them to it, and that a lasting abode in it awaits them. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, like Ibn 'Atiyya, take the burden to mean sin and disbelief, while al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi understand it as a crushing punishment, likened to a load that breaks the back of the one who carries it. On the grammar of the verb sā'a, al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi see an implicit pronoun explained by the accusative 'ḥimlan', with the object of dispraise left unstated, namely 'their burden'. Abu al-Su'ud and al-Alusi accept the sense of 'to grieve' but judge it to fit the context poorly. On the meaning of remaining forever, al-Qurtubi and the Jalalayn take it as the punishment itself, while Abu al-Su'ud takes it as the continual bearing of the burden. Ibn Sa'di adds that the deeds themselves turn into punishment for their doers. The verse thus concludes the story of Moses as a warning against turning away from the divine reminder.

This verse describes the Day when the Trumpet is blown and God gathers the criminals, their eyes blue with dread. The commentators differ on the meaning of "zurqan". Al-Tabari, al-Mawardi, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi report that it refers to a disfiguring pale blue colour of the eyes, which the Arabs disliked because the Byzantines, their enemies, had blue eyes. Al-Farra' and al-Kalbi take it to mean blindness, while al-Zajjaj and al-Azhari explain it as thirst, which turns the pupil bluish. Abu Muslim sees a fixed, staring gaze born of fear, and others see a discoloration of the whole body. Ibn 'Abbas, as cited by al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, held that the Day of Judgement has several stages, in some of which they will be blue-eyed and in others blind, a view that many commentators accept as reconciling the verses.

The word "yatakhafatun" means that they speak to one another in hushed tones out of terror. The phrase "in labithtum illa ashra" has two main readings. Al-Hasan and Qatada say it refers to their stay in this world. Others say it refers to their time in the graves, or to the interval between the two blasts, said by some to be forty years. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi note that they regard that period as short, either from longing for happy days or in comparison with the endless Hereafter. Al-Baydawi and al-Qurtubi add that the wisest of them says they stayed only one day, which expresses how brief the time seemed. Readers also differ on whether the verb is "nanfukh" (We blow) or "yunfakh" (it is blown), with most adopting the passive form.

This verse describes the state of the wrongdoers on the Day of Resurrection, when the Trumpet is blown and they are gathered with blue, that is, pale-eyed, faces. They speak to one another in hushed tones, and one of them says that they only remained ten nights. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi agree that the verb means whispering, and that the terror filling their chests is the reason. The meaning of zurqan is debated. Al-Tabari and al-Baghawi take it as intense thirst or blindness, al-Mawardi lists six views including blindness, a disfigured appearance, a fixed stare, and a false hope that turns to disappointment, while al-Zamakhshari notes that blue eyes were the colour the Arabs disliked most. On the length of the ten, scholars differ. Al-Hasan and Qatada take it as their life in this world, others as their stay in the graves, and Ibn Abbas, as reported by Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Qurtubi, as the interval between the two blasts. Al-Razi, Ibn Kathir and al-Baydawi note that God prefers the view of the most intelligent among them, who says they stayed only a single day. Ibn 'Ashur sees in the figure of ten an attempt to excuse their denial of resurrection. The commentators agree that the scene conveys the gravity of the Day of Judgment and how brief the life of this world appears in that moment.

God knows best what they murmur when the most judicious of them says: you stayed only a single day. The commentators explain that on that day the guilty will be gathered with blue eyes, which some take as blindness, others as the thirst-dulled gaze, and others as eyes fixed in terror. They will speak in hushed tones from the dread filling their hearts, and say: you stayed only ten days. The commentators agree that this underestimation comes from the horror of the scene and from the shortness of worldly life in their eyes, but they differ on where that stay was. Al-Hasan, Qatada, al-Dahhak and Muqatil, as well as al-Tabari, say it refers to life in this world. Others, including Mujahid-based reports and al-Baghawi, say it refers to the time in the graves. Ibn Abbas, al-Qurtubi and Ibn al-Jawzi also report the interval between the two blasts, forty years. Ibn Kathir, al-Baydawi and Abu al-Su'ud hold that the whole of worldly life seems brief next to the eternal hereafter.

Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn Atiyya and al-Razi note that the one who says a single day is preferred by God, not because he is closer to the truth, as Abu al-Su'ud clarifies, but because his words better reveal the severity of the terror. Al-Tabari, al-Razi and al-Alusi observe that the word day here means any span of time, and its indefiniteness conveys smallness.

The passage then turns to the mountains, which God will blow away, leaving the earth level and bare. Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and most exegetes understand the crookedness and the rises as dips and mounds, while al-Tabari emphasizes deviation and bending. Scholars differ on these terms, yet they agree on the central image of a flattened earth.

The verse reports that people ask the Prophet about the fate of the mountains, and God commands him to answer that his Lord will blow them away as dust. According to most commentators, they will first be ground into sand, then become like carded wool carried by the winds, until they are scattered as dust. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Atiyya agree that the earth will then be left flat and smooth, bare of vegetation, a qa' safsaf. They differ on the meaning of awaj and amt. Ibn Abbas and Qatada take them as valleys and hills, or crack and mound; Mujahid as depression and elevation; Ibn Kathir prefers the latter, while al-Tabari judges that awaj means a slight inclination and amt a slight bend or weakness, so that there will be neither dip nor rise. Al-Razi and Ibn al-Jawzi relate that a man from Thaqif asked the Prophet about it. Al-Zamakhshari notes that the choice of the kasra form of awaj, usually reserved for abstract matters, conveys a level so perfect that only geometric measurement could detect any irregularity. The commentators add that people will follow the caller's voice without deviating, that voices will be hushed so that only a whisper is heard, which some take as the sound of footsteps and others as quiet speech. Finally, intercession will profit only those whom the All-Merciful permits and whose words He approves, which Ibn Abbas identifies as the declaration that there is no god but God.

This passage describes the crushing of the mountains on the Day of Resurrection. When asked about the mountains, God tells His Prophet to say that his Lord will scatter them like sand and then like windblown dust, leaving the earth as a level, smooth plain, qa'an safsafan, with no vegetation or structures. The commentators largely agree on this meaning. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi explain that qa' means flat ground and safsaf means smooth terrain without plants, with Ibn Kathir seeing the second word as an emphasis on the first. As for the pronoun in 'fayadharuha', some refer it to the mountains, meaning their places, as al-Baydawi and Abu al-Su'ud do, while others, such as al-Shinqiti and al-Nasafi, refer it to the earth even though it was not mentioned. On 'iwajan wa la amtan', opinions differ. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, al-Hasan and Qatada take them as valleys and hills, or as lows and highs, or as cracks and mounds. Al-Tabari prefers that awaj means inclination and amt a slight protrusion, so that the earth has neither rise nor dip. Al-Zamakhshari argues that the kasra in 'iwaj' suits what is known only by geometric measurement, while Ibn 'Ashur holds the two forms to be synonyms. The commentators then describe the gathering, where people follow the caller without deviation, and voices fall so silent that only a whisper is heard, which most take to be the sound of footsteps, others a low speech. Ibn al-Jawzi reports that the revelation was prompted by a question from a man of Thaqif.

These verses describe the fate of the mountains on the Day of Resurrection. God uproots them and grinds them down until they become like sand and then like scattered dust, leaving the earth as a levelled, smooth plain without vegetation, in which the observer sees no crookedness and no rise. The commentators agree on the general sense: al-'iwaj means curvature or deviation, and al-amt means a slight protuberance. They differ on the details. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, al-Hasan and Ibn Kathir explain that al-'iwaj is the valley or hollow and al-amt the hill or height, while Qatada takes al-'iwaj as a crack and al-amt as a small mound. Another report from Ibn 'Abbas gives al-'iwaj the sense of inclination and al-amt that of a trace like a sandal strap. Al-Tabari prefers the meaning of inclination, since that is the usage of the Arabs, and takes al-amt as bending or weakness, so that the verse denies both rising and falling. Al-Zamakhshari notes that the vowel form with a short vowel is used for abstract things, and that this form suits an irregularity so subtle that it can only be detected by geometric measurement; al-Baydawi, al-Nasafi and Abu al-Su'ud follow him. The passage then turns to the crowd following the summoner without deviation, and to voices hushed until only a whisper is heard, which most understand as the sound of footsteps, others as quiet speech or moving lips.

This verse describes the Day of Judgment, when the mountains are blown away: people follow the caller toward the place of assembly and do not deviate from him. Most commentators, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi, identify the caller as Israfil and explain that people cannot turn away from his summons and hurry toward it. Ibn Atiyya notes that the phrase can mean either that the call is true beyond doubt or that no one can escape following it.

On the word "khashi'a" (to be humbled, to fall silent), Ibn Abbas and Ibn Kathir say voices become still in submission before the Most Merciful, while al-Razi and al-Zamakhshari describe voices lowered out of fear and awe.

The meaning of "hams" is disputed. Ibn Abbas, Ikrima, al-Hasan, Ibn Jubayr, al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj take it as the sound of feet walking to the gathering place. Mujahid, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi take it as speech spoken in a low voice, and some as lip movement without sound, supported by a reading attributed to Ubayy ibn Ka'b. Ibn Kathir combines both views, saying hushed speech may occur in some moments and not in others.

The commentators also discuss the levelled earth with no "iwaj" or "amt": Ibn Abbas understands valleys and hills, al-Hasan and Mujahid dips and rises, while al-Tabari reads it as slight bending or unevenness. Al-Zamakhshari explains that the precision of the wording expresses the total flatness of the ground.

This verse states that on the Day of Judgment intercession will benefit no one except the one whom the Most Merciful has permitted to intercede and whose words He approves. The commentators agree that intercession happens only by God's permission and that the person interceded for must be one whose words and deeds God accepts. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Juzayy, as well as al-Baghawi, take the approved word to be the testimony that there is no god but God, and Ibn Abbas is reported to say the same. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi read the particle li as giving the reason: God approves the intercessor's speech for the sake of the one he intercedes for. Abu Hayyan and Ibn 'Atiyya allow several grammatical readings of the word man and of the exception, presenting them without choosing between them. Al-Razi notes that the verse is a strong argument for the intercession of believers who have committed sins, and he reports the Mu'tazilite view that rejects it. As for the phrase that God knows what lies before and behind them, al-Tabari and al-Razi refer it to the angels, while others refer it to the created beings or to those who follow the caller. All of them see in this passage a portrayal of the greatness of that day and the humility of every creature before God.

This verse states that God alone knows what lies before people and what lies behind them, and that created beings cannot encompass His knowledge. The commentators differ on the reference of the pronouns. Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, and al-Mahalli with al-Suyuti take what is before them to be the matters of the Hereafter and what is behind them to be the affairs of this world. Al-Tabari holds that the pronoun refers to the angels: God knows what lies before and behind the angels, but the angels do not know it, and the verse rebukes those who worshipped angels. Al-Razi, al-Baydawi, al-Nasafi and al-Alusi prefer that the pronoun refers to the things before and behind, as the nearest antecedent, so that people cannot grasp those matters with knowledge. Ibn al-Qayyim argues that the first reading implies the second but not the reverse. Ibn Juzayy holds that the meaning is that people cannot grasp God's essence. Al-Shawkani and Ibn Kathir see the pronoun as referring to God, so that no one can encompass His knowledge or essence. Ibn Ashur and Sa'di place the verse within a description of the terrors of the Day of Judgment, when no intercession is granted except by God's permission. Ibn 'Atiyya stresses that God's knowledge encompasses all things. Ibn Kathir compares the verse to the statement in Surat al-Baqara about God's knowledge.

This verse says that on the Day of Judgment faces will be humbled and submit before the Living, the Self-Subsisting, who never dies and who sustains all creation, and that whoever carries injustice has lost. The commentators agree on the meaning of 'anat: to be humbled and submissive, from which the word for a captive, 'ani, derives. Ibn 'Abbas and Qatada explain it as being abased, Mujahid as being humbled in reverence, and Tabari adds the sense of yielding. Talq ibn Habib understands it as prostration, with forehead and nose on the ground, and Ibn Juzayy restricts it to the Day of Resurrection. Ibn Kathir says that all creatures submit to the Living who never sleeps.

Most scholars take 'injustice' (dhulm) to mean polytheism, as Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada and Ibn Zayd say, and Ibn Kathir cites the verse that shirk is a great injustice. Mawardi holds that it covers polytheism and all sins, so the loss is proportionate to what one carries. Zamakhshari treats the sentence as a parenthesis describing the loss of the sinners, while Ibn 'Atiyya sees it as contrasting with the believers. As for the 'faces', Zamakhshari, Abu al-Su'ud and Alusi take them to be those of the guilty, while others understand all faces.

The next verse concerns the believer who does good deeds and fears neither injustice nor diminution. Ibn 'Abbas, Hasan and Qatada explain that no sin is added to his record and no good deed taken from it, and Dahhak adds that he is not punished for a sin he did not commit. Ibn Kathir notes that Ibn Kathir reads the verb in the jussive as a prohibition, while the other readers use the indicative. Razi and Mawardi clarify that hadm means a reduction in reward.

This verse states that whoever does good deeds while being a believer will fear, on the Day of Resurrection, neither injustice, meaning that sins not committed would be added to his record, nor diminution, meaning that some of his good deeds would be taken away. Al-Tabari understands the good deeds as the religious obligations, while al-Razi takes them to be all good actions. Ibn Juzayy and Abu Hayyan note that the particle "min" indicates a part, since no one can perform all good deeds. Most commentators, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Mahalli, agree that injustice means the addition of sins and diminution the loss of good deeds. Ibn Kathir adds that injustice here means being burdened with another's sin. Ibn Zayd, and Ibn 'Atiyya in one of his explanations, hold instead that the believer does not fear being left unrewarded for his deeds. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya report that injustice is taking more than one's due, and diminution is withholding what is owed to another. Al-Mawardi distinguishes injustice, the denial of the whole right, from diminution, the denial of part of it. Ibn 'Ashur holds that injustice can be a severe loss and diminution a slight one. Regarding the reading of Ibn Kathir, "fala yakhaf" in the jussive as a prohibition, al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and al-Shinqiti accept that it conveys the same meaning, the prohibition serving as a reassurance.

This verse states that God sent down the Quran in clear Arabic and varied its warnings, so that people might guard themselves against shirk and sin, or that the Quran might create in them a reminder and a lesson. The commentators explain that the warnings are the accounts of earlier nations that rejected their messengers and the descriptions of punishment, and that taqwa means refraining from wrongdoing. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi take the phrase about creating a reminder to mean caution, piety and taking heed from past examples, while Ibn Atiyya, al-Nasafi and al-Zamakhshari add the sense of honour and nobility that faith brings. Some, following the usage of the word dhikr, understand it as obedience and worship. Al-Razi and al-Baydawi note that the action is ascribed to people for taqwa and to the Quran for the new reminder it produces. Readings differ on the verb, but without changing the overall meaning. The following verses, which tell the Prophet not to hasten the recitation before Gabriel finishes and to ask for more knowledge, are linked by Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi to his eagerness to memorise. Al-Qurtubi and others mention other occasions of revelation, but most stress this motive. The commentators do not settle between these readings and present them side by side.

God instructs His Prophet not to hasten in receiving and reciting the Qur'an before the angel has finished delivering it, and to ask his Lord for more knowledge. The commentators first note that God is exalted above every imperfection and above what the polytheists say. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn al-Jawzi, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi explain that the prohibition concerns rushing to recite along with Gabriel for fear of forgetting, as the verse 'Move not your tongue to hasten it' also shows; he should listen and wait until the angel finishes, then recite. Mujahid and Qatada give another reading: he should not teach or dictate the Qur'an to people before its meaning is made clear to him, a view also reported by al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and al-Shawkani. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and al-Baydawi understand the prohibition as haste in receiving the revelation and competing to recite with the angel, and see the request for more knowledge as showing that knowledge is what should be sought more. Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Qurtubi and al-Shawkani report several occasions of revelation, including the story of the man who slapped his wife, though al-Razi, al-Baydawi and Ibn Kathir consider that report weak or do not rely on it. The commentators agree on the recommendation to ask God for more knowledge and on the value of patience and careful listening in learning.

God recalls that He had earlier made a covenant with Adam, commanding him not to approach the forbidden tree; Adam forgot the commitment and God found no firm resolve in him. The commentators see in the verse a consolation for the Prophet ﷺ: forgetting and breaching a covenant is old among the children of Adam, and their father himself fell into it. On the meaning of 'fa-nasiya', al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Mujahid and al-Hasan take it as neglect or abandonment of the command, while others, including Ibn Abbas in one transmission, keep the literal sense of forgetfulness, which some view as an excuse and others as carelessness. Ibn 'Atiyya argues that mere forgetting cannot be meant here, since the forgetful person is not held to account. As for 'azm', most explain it as patience (Qatada, Muqatil), keeping the command (Ibn Abbas, Ibn Zayd, Ata') or firm resolve (Abu Hayyan, al-Zamakhshari), with al-Zamakhshari adding that it must be firm enough to discourage Satan. Some, such as al-Nasafi, conclude from the verse that Adam was not among the steadfast messengers, while others present it as praise of Adam's forbearance, which according to a hadith outweighs that of all his descendants. Ibn Sa'di notes that man is called 'insan' because he forgets, and that Adam's prompt repentance is a model. Al-Shinqiti observes that scholars differ on whether forgetfulness excuses the sinner, and that prophets are protected from faults concerning the transmission of the message.

This verse recalls God's command to the angels to prostrate before Adam: all of them obeyed except Iblis, who refused out of pride. The commentators generally see the story as a reminder that follows the mention of Adam's forgetfulness, showing Iblis's enmity towards him. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir explain that God warns Adam not to obey this enemy, lest he expel them both from Paradise and he become wretched. Ibn Atiyya, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Zamakhshari note that the singular form of the verb for hardship refers to Adam because he was the head of the household and the one who worked, so he bore the greater toil. Al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir take this hardship to mean tilling, sowing, grinding and baking, and cite the report from Sa'id ibn Jubayr about a red bull Adam used to plough with. Paradise is described as a place without hunger, nakedness, thirst or the heat of the sun. On Iblis's nature, Ibn 'Abbas, al-Nasafi and al-Baydawi hold that he was a jinn who worshipped God alongside the angels, while al-Hasan distinguishes the angels' nature from his fiery origin. Others say he belonged to the angels, which would make the exception continuous. As for the word 'abā', al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and Abu Hayyan treat the clause as a new sentence showing that the refusal stemmed from arrogance, with its object either left implied or treated as intransitive. Ibn Kathir also cites the authentic hadith in which Moses argues with Adam.

The commentators explain that after Iblis refused to prostrate to Adam, God warned Adam that this one is an enemy to him and to his wife. They must not obey him, lest he cause their expulsion from the Garden, and then Adam would suffer hardship. Most exegetes take this hardship to mean the toil of earning a living: ploughing, reaping, grinding and baking. The Garden, by contrast, is a place free from hunger, nakedness, thirst and the heat of the sun.

Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir transmit the report from Sa'id ibn Jubayr that a red bull was sent down to Adam, which he used to plough while wiping the sweat from his brow. Al-Sam'ani and al-Baghawi repeat this report, and Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Qurtubi also cite it, with al-Qurtubi adding another account in which Adam chased a loaf of bread that rolled from his hand. Al-Mawardi, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Razi note that the verb is singular, not dual, because the labour falls mainly on the man, who earns the living. Al-Zamakhshari adds that the man's hardship includes that of his household.

Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Ashur read the hardship as daily fatigue. Al-Razi links this passage to the story's sequence, recalling that Adam had forgotten the covenant. Abu Hayyan and al-Shawkani record the variant readings of the following verses. Al-Alusi remarks on the repetition of the preposition before the wife, which stresses the enmity, while Ibn Sa'di dwells on the abundance of the Garden. Modern writers such as Sayyid Qutb and al-Sha'rawi focus on the man's responsibility for providing for the household.

The commentators explain that this verse lists the blessings granted to Adam in Paradise: he will neither go hungry nor be naked, neither thirst nor be exposed to the heat of the midday sun, and these gifts last as long as he remains there. Hunger and nakedness are paired with thirst and the heat of the sun, and Ibn al-Qayyim sees a precise contrast in which hunger is inner pain, nakedness outer pain, thirst inner heat and dhuha outer heat, so the verse negates every affliction. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir explain that dhuha means being struck by the sun, and Ikrima adds that there is no sun in Paradise, its people dwelling in extended shade. The major exegetes agree that these four needs are the essential supports of human life, granted in Paradise without seeking or labour. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Alusi see in the separation of these pairs a rhetorical device for enumerating each blessing distinctly and for matching the verse endings. On the recitation, Nafi' and Abu Bakr through 'Asim read wa inna with a kasra, while the others read it with a fatha, and al-Tabari prefers the latter. Several commentators connect the verse to the hardship of earthly life: al-Razi, al-Qurtubi and Ibn 'Ashur see in the warning about toil the labour of ploughing and sowing, and Sa'id ibn Jubayr mentions the red ox that worked for Adam. The address is to Adam alone because he bears the duty of earning a living.

The commentators explain that God tells Adam that in Paradise he will neither hunger nor go naked, nor thirst nor be struck by the heat of the sun, meaning that he will have his food, clothing and shelter without toil or hardship. Ibn 'Abbas and most exegetes, including al-Tabari, take the phrase "nor be exposed to the sun" literally, while Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi note that there is no sun in Paradise and its people dwell in extended shade. The verse is generally linked to the warning against Satan, since leaving Paradise would bring the hardship of working the land. On the reading, all agree that "wa anna-ka" with a fatha is coordinated with "allā tajū'", whereas Nafi' and Abu Bakr read it with a kasra as a new clause or as coordinated with "inna laka"; al-Tabari prefers the fatha. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn al-Qayyim highlight the rhetorical beauty of the arrangement, which pairs hunger with nakedness and thirst with the sun's heat, matching inner and outer discomfort, and lists each blessing separately. Commentators agree that these verses describe Adam's state before disobedience, without judging between the differing accounts of the temptation and the nature of the tree.

This verse tells that Satan whispered to Adam, offering to guide him to the tree of eternity and to a kingdom that never decays. The commentators agree on the meaning of waswasa as a secret, enticing suggestion, and that Satan linked the tree to immortality because whoever ate from it, as was claimed, would not die. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi report, through Ibn 'Abbas, al-Suddi and Qatada, that the tree granted life without end and a rule that would not fade, a promise that was false. Al-Razi, al-Qadi and Ibn 'Atiyya hold that the whispering was an audible exchange of words, while others think it was an idea inserted into the soul; al-Qurtubi favours a direct exchange, following the plain wording. The commentators also agree that the specific tree is not known with certainty, so identifying it adds little. Scholars differ on the sense of the word yabla: some render it as not perishing, others as not wearing out or not ceasing. Most say this promise was the reason Adam ate from the forbidden tree, and al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi stress the lure of immortality and power. Ibn 'Ashur explains that the question is an offer, and that Satan pointed not to the forbidden tree but to another, so Adam came to think it would grant him eternity. The commentaries therefore take the verse as a warning against being seduced by the desire for long life and power.

This verse tells that Adam and Eve ate from the forbidden tree, and their private parts became visible to them after having been hidden from them. They began pressing leaves of the Garden onto themselves to cover up, and Adam disobeyed his Lord and went astray. Most commentators, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Baydawi, explain that Satan enticed them to eat with the promise of eternal life and a kingdom that never decays. Most understand the word 'went astray' as losing the goal they sought, namely immortality, or as deviating from the right path. Ibn Qutayba holds that one may say Adam disobeyed but not that he was a disobedient person, just as one who sews a garment is said to have sewn it without being called a tailor. Al-Razi, al-Qurtubi and al-Alusi report the scholars' answers on the question of prophetic sin: some place the act before prophethood, others regard it as a minor lapse or the omission of what was better. Al-Zamakhshari, however, stresses the sharp rebuke conveyed by the wording and rejects the reading that 'went astray' means he overate. On the leaves, Mujahid and Qatada say they were stitched together like a garment, while Ibn Abbas and Said ibn Jubayr identify them as fig leaves. The verse ends by stating that God chose Adam after his lapse, granted him repentance and guided him, which the commentators understand as election and the help to repent.

This verse says that after Adam disobeyed and went astray, his Lord chose him and drew him near, accepted his repentance, and guided him to remain steadfast in it. The commentators agree that election (ijtiba') means choosing and bringing close, that repentance (tawba) is God's acceptance of Adam's return from his sin, and that guidance (huda) is the enabling of Adam to persevere in repentance and hold fast to the means of protection. Al-Tabari explains that the election came after the disobedience and that God granted Adam the return to what pleases Him. Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Baydawi and al-Alusi note that the root of the word carries the sense of gathering and selecting. Al-Shinqiti links the repentance to the words Adam received from his Lord, as mentioned in the Surah of the Cow.

Opinions differ on the nature of the sin. Al-Razi and Ibn Fawrak hold that it happened before prophethood, while al-Qurtubi reports that it can be regarded as a minor fault or as leaving what is more excellent, and Ibn 'Ashur judges that Adam was not yet a prophet and that this passage neither permits nor forbids sin in prophets. Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi cite the hadith of the debate between Adam and Moses, in which Adam prevails because God had decreed the act before creating him. Al-Sha'rawi avoids this debate and sees the election as the start of Adam's prophethood.

The commentators explain that the verse addresses Adam and Eve, and some hold that Iblis is included with them, while others take it as addressing Adam and his descendants along with Iblis and his. It concerns the descent from the Garden to the earth, and the enmity between the two sides remains. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi understand this enmity as rivalry in worldly affairs, and al-Nasafi also sees religious opposition in it. All agree that the guidance mentioned is the clear direction sent by God through the Books and the messengers, and that whoever follows it will not go astray in this world nor be wretched in the next. Ibn 'Abbas reports that God guaranteed this to whoever recites the Quran and acts by it, a view supported by al-Sha'bi and many others. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya explain wretchedness as the punishment for straying in the afterlife, so that not being wretched follows from not straying. Al-Razi holds that guidance includes evidence and acting upon it, and that the negation is general, in this life and the next.

As for one who turns away from the remembrance, he will have a constricted life. The commentators differ widely on what this constricted life means. Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ikrima and al-Dahhak take it as unlawful gain or impure provision; al-Hasan, Qatada and Ibn Zayd take it as zaqqum and dari' in Hell; Ibn Mas'ud, Abu Sa'id al-Khudri and Abu Hurayra, followed by al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Razi, take it as the punishment of the grave and its squeezing. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Razi report other views, such as anxiety and narrowness of life in this world. The blind gathering is understood by Ibn 'Abbas and al-Zamakhshari as physical blindness, and by Mujahid as blindness to proof.

The verse thus makes plain that following guidance leads to security, while turning away from it brings constriction and blindness.

The commentators explain that turning away from the remembrance of God means turning away from the Qur'an and the guidance brought by the messengers, by not believing in it and not acting upon it. Whoever does so will have a constricted and hard life, without peace of heart or ease of mind, even if he is given wealth and comfort. He will be raised on the Day of Resurrection blind. They differ on the kind of blindness: Ibn Abbas and Mujahid take it as blindness to the proof, an inability to find the argument, while others understand physical blindness, the view al-Tabari, Ibn al-Qayyim and Ibn Kathir favour, reconciling the two states according to the moment. As for the constricted life, many early scholars linked it to the punishment of the grave, as reported from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri and Ibn Mas'ud, and al-Tabari considered this the soundest reading, supported by the mention of the Hereafter's punishment that follows. Others took it as hardship in this world, caused by greed, miserliness and bad opinion of God, or as unlawful earnings, according to Ikrima and al-Dahhak, or as the punishment of Hell with its thorny plant and zaqqum, according to al-Hasan and Qatada. Some combine these meanings, holding that the constricted life covers this world, the barzakh and the Hereafter. Al-Zamakhshari and others note the contrast: faith brings contentment even in hardship. Ibn Kathir adds that forgetting the Qur'an after memorising it carries a separate warning.

The commentators explain that whoever turns away from the remembrance of God, that is from His Book and His guidance, will have a constricted life in this world, even when his means are ample, and will be raised on the Day of Resurrection blind. He will ask his Lord in bewilderment why he was raised blind when he had been seeing. God will answer that His signs came to him and he forgot them, and that just as he forgot them, he is now forgotten in punishment. The exegetes agree that the recompense is of the same kind as the deed. As to the meaning of the constricted life, most explain daank as narrowness and hardship; Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid take it as misery or a straitened livelihood, while 'Ikrima and al-Dahhak speak of unlawful gain or corrupt sustenance. Regarding the constricted life itself, Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, Abu Hurayra and Ibn Mas'ud identify it with the punishment of the grave, al-Hasan and Qatada with the thorny plant and zaqqum in the Fire, and others with the narrowing of worldly circumstances for the disbeliever who thinks ill of God. On blindness, Mujahid reads it as blindness to the proof, while others take it as blindness of sight; Ibn 'Abbas reports that the one raised sees at first and becomes blind when driven to the place of gathering. Al-Tabari understands 'I was seeing' as seeing by the proof or by things in the life of this world, and notes that the questioner is ignorant of the sin that brought this about. The readings differ in the vowelling of a'mā and in the imāla of the alif.

The commentators explain that this verse is God's answer to the one who turned away from His remembrance. Raised up blind on the Day of Resurrection, he asks why he was gathered blind when he had been seeing. He is told that, just as Our signs came to him and he forgot them, so today he is forgotten. The punishment thus matches the deed. Most, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Nasafi and al-Jalalayn, agree that forgetting here means abandoning and neglecting, not mere lapse of memory, and that he will be left in the Fire. Qatada adds that they forgot the good but not the punishment. Ibn Juzayy and Ibn Ashur read it as a figure for being deprived of mercy. The preceding verse about a constricted life has been read in several ways. Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and al-Dahhak take it as hardship in this world or unlawful gain, al-Hasan and Qatada as the thorny plant and the zaqqum in Hell, while Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, Ibn Mas'ud and Abu Hurayra take it as the punishment of the grave, an opinion al-Tabari prefers. On blindness, Mujahid understands blindness to the proof, others physical blindness, and al-Tabari holds it general. Beyond stating their preferences, the commentators do not settle these differences.

The commentators explain that this verse warns those who commit excesses and do not believe in the signs of their Lord that they will receive a similar recompense, and that the punishment of the Hereafter is more severe and more lasting. Most agree that the excess here means associating partners with God or persistent transgression of the prohibitions, and that not believing in the signs is an explanation of that excess. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi stress that the lasting quality of the Hereafter's punishment lies in its never ending, whereas the suffering of this world comes to an end.

Opinions differ on the "narrowed life" mentioned just before. Ibn Mas'ud, Abu Sa'id al-Khudri and al-Suddi understand it as the punishment of the grave, al-Hasan and Qatada as the Zaqqum and thorny plants of Hell, while Ibn 'Abbas and 'Ata' understand it as the anguish that the disbeliever feels even when he is materially comfortable. Others take it to mean unlawful gain or wealth without fear of God. Al-Razi reports these views and notes that they may all be combined.

As for the blindness on the Day of Resurrection, Ibn 'Abbas and 'Ikrima understand physical blindness, Mujahid blindness to the proof, and al-Jubba'i an inability to find the right path. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Ashur see in the contrast between this world and the Hereafter an emphasis on the lasting nature of the final punishment.

This verse rebukes the polytheists for failing to draw a lesson from the peoples God destroyed before them. As they travel, they pass through the dwellings of those generations and see the traces of their ruin, and these traces are signs for people of understanding. Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Baghawi report that the addressees are the Quraysh, who traded with Syria and passed the homes of 'Ad, Thamud and the towns of Lot. Tabari judges this reading the soundest, while acknowledging that others have a valid view. Ibn Kathir widens the meaning to all the nations that rejected their messengers, and urges reflection on their remains. The commentators differ over the subject of the verb 'yahdi': the Kufans and al-Zamakhshari take the following clause as subject, Baydawi and al-Nasafi take it to be God, supported by the reading 'nahdi' in the first person plural, and others supply an implied subject such as guidance or reflection. On the meaning of 'al-nuha', Tabari says it means intellect, Qatada says people of piety, and Razi notes that it denotes reason that restrains from vices. As for the following phrase, most commentators take the 'prior word' to be the postponement of punishment until the Last Day or the day of Badr, and the 'appointed term' to be the fixed time of their chastisement, with Ibn Kathir adding that God punishes no one before the proof has been established.

The commentators explain that the peoples destroyed before were punished, while Quraysh was not, because of a prior decree of God that postponed their punishment. Ibn Kathir, al-Baydawi and Ibn 'Ashur take this decree to be God's promise to delay the chastisement of this community until the Hereafter, and al-Zamakhshari and al-Qasimi read it similarly as a deferred recompense. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir understand the word lizam as the inevitable doom, with Ibn 'Abbas explaining it as death and Ibn Zayd as killing. As for the appointed term, al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir refer it to the life of this world or to the Hour, while Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn al-Jawzi also mention the day of Badr, which al-Bukhari reports, and Qatada links it to the Day of Resurrection. Al-Razi holds that the decree was a divine announcement to the angels, and that its wisdom is hidden from God's knowledge, according to the people of the Sunna. Regarding the command to be patient and to glorify God, most exegetes, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi, identify the times with the five daily prayers: dawn, afternoon, evening and night, and midday. Al-Razi and al-Baydawi offer other divisions. On the reading of 'tarda', al-Tabari regards both readings as correct and equivalent, one meaning that you may be pleased with the reward, the other that God may be pleased with you.

God instructs His Prophet to bear patiently the words of his opponents, who called him a sorcerer, a poet or a madman, and to glorify his Lord with praise at set times. Most commentators understand these as the five daily prayers: the dawn prayer before sunrise, the afternoon prayer before sunset, part of the night for maghrib and 'isha', and midday prayer, which falls at the two ends of the day. The aim is that he may be pleased with his reward. The commentators agree that the verse has an inverted order: the earlier word of God and the appointed term are what delayed the punishment, for otherwise it would have struck them at once. On the meaning of 'lizam', al-Tabari reports from Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Zayd that it means death or killing, while Qatada identifies the appointed term as the Day of Judgment and others as the Battle of Badr. Regarding the reading of 'turda', the majority read it with a fatha, meaning he will be content with what he receives, whereas 'Asim (through Abu Bakr) and al-Kisa'i read it with a damma, meaning his Lord will content him; al-Tabari holds both readings to be equivalent. According to al-Kalbi and Muqatil the verse is abrogated by the verse of fighting, but others consider it still in force. Scholars also differ on the 'extremities of the day': some say it means midday alone, others dawn and maghrib, or dawn, noon and afternoon, and the plural form is explained as avoiding ambiguity. Glorifying God is understood by many as prayer, while Abu Muslim and al-Razi prefer to read it as declaring God free of all imperfection.

God tells His Prophet not to gaze long at the wealth He has given some disbelievers, for it is only the fleeting splendour of this life, through which they are tested, while the provision of his Lord is better and more lasting. The commentators agree that the "pairs" are kinds or types among the disbelievers, that the "flower" is adornment and brightness, and that the purpose of these things is trial. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi hold that a passing glance is excused and that the prohibition concerns admiration and longing, whereas al-Qasimi and Ibn 'Ashur take lengthening the gaze itself as the target. Opinions differ on the "provision": al-Tabari and al-Baghawi take it as the reward of the Hereafter, al-Mawardi and Abu Hayyan as contentment, al-Zamakhshari as what is lawful, and al-Razi and Ibn 'Atiyya as the conquests and spoils God grants the believers. The report that the Prophet borrowed food from a Jew and offered his armour as surety is cited by al-Tabari and al-Baghawi, but Ibn 'Atiyya, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi regard it with doubt since the surah is Meccan. Several scholars, including Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi, draw from the verse that one should command one's household to pray and rely on God for sustenance, since the good end belongs to the God-conscious.

God instructs His Prophet ﷺ to command his family to pray and to persevere in it himself. He tells him that He asks no provision from him, neither for himself nor for others, since it is God who provides for him, and that the good outcome belongs to those who are mindful of God. The commentators understand “his family” as either his kin or his people, and some include all who follow him within his community, as al-Mawardi, Ibn al-Jawzi, al-Baghawi and al-Baydawi note. They agree that “endure” means to persist in prayer, and that God takes charge of the sustenance of the Prophet and his household so that he can devote himself to the Hereafter. Ibn Kathir reports that provision comes from unexpected places to one who keeps up the prayer. Several scholars note that prayer is a refuge in hardship, and they cite reports attributed to 'Urwa ibn al-Zubayr, Bakr al-Muzani and 'Umar ibn al-Khattab. Al-Razi and Ibn 'Atiyya see in the verse an invitation for believers to teach their households and help them worship. On the meaning of “the good outcome,” Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid take it as the salvation of those who believed the Messenger, while others take it as Paradise or a praiseworthy end in this life and the next. Al-Razi and al-Nasafi clarify that the verse does not permit abandoning work, but asks that the heart be freed for worship. Ibn 'Ashur explains that the denial of any request for provision cancels the tributes people were accustomed to paying to rulers, and that worship itself is gratitude to God.

This verse reports the demand of the Meccan disbelievers: why does Muhammad not bring us a sign from his Lord, as earlier prophets did, such as the she-camel of Salih or Jesus healing the blind and the leper? God answers that the greatest sign has already come to them, namely the Qur'an, which bears witness to what is in the earlier scriptures, the accounts of past nations. Most commentators regard the Qur'an as the greatest and most lasting miracle, since a miracle is an extraordinary event granted to one who claims prophethood, and this book came through an unlettered man who had neither studied nor learned from the People of the Book. Al-Tabari, Mujahid, Qatada, Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn Kathir explain that the earlier scrolls are the Torah and the Gospel, which contain the promise of the Prophet. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi, Abu al-Su'ud and al-Alusi hold that the Qur'an itself is the proof, since the earlier books need its testimony to be confirmed. Ibn Kathir and al-Tabari also mention that the destruction of nations who asked for signs and then denied them is a warning. Readers differ on whether the verb is feminine or masculine. The verse ends with a warning: each side awaits, and you will know who follows the straight path and who is guided.

The verse says that if God had destroyed these disbelievers with punishment before sending the Prophet and revealing the Quran, they would have said on the Day of Resurrection: 'Our Lord, why did You not send us a messenger, so that we could follow Your signs before we were humbled and disgraced?' Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Jalalayn read this as a plea they will make in the Hereafter. Some take the pronoun in 'before it' to refer to the Prophet, others to the clear proof or to the Quran. Ibn Kathir notes that the Quran is itself the greatest sign given to the Prophet, so no excuse remains once it has been revealed. Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn 'Ashur hold that the verse establishes the argument against them, since the messenger has now come.

Al-Razi, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Tabari cite the hadith of Abu Sa'id about the three who will plead before God on the Day of Resurrection: the one who died in the interval between prophets, the person deprived of reason, and the young child. Ibn 'Atiyya argues that the Quraysh were not people of such an interval because they had heard of prophecy, while al-Qadi questions the soundness of the report. On the words dhull and khizy, al-Baydawi and al-Qurtubi, citing Ibn 'Abbas, take dhull as worldly humiliation by killing and captivity and khizy as entry into Hell, whereas al-Jalalayn places both in the Hereafter. Some readers vocalised the verbs in the passive.

As for 'Say: each is waiting', al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir understand that both sides await the outcome. Al-Mawardi suggests waiting for victory or for the truth to become manifest. Al-Razi considers that the waiting may be for death, for reward and punishment after death, and explains that the question 'you will know' is a warning rather than an expression of doubt.

God instructs His Prophet ﷺ to say to the disbelievers: each of us is waiting for the outcome of this matter, so wait, for you will soon know who are the people of the upright path, meaning the straight road with no crookedness, and who has been guided. The commentators agree that this verse is a warning and threat that closes the passage. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir explain that the polytheists said they were waiting for the turns of fate to take the Prophet, so that after his death they would be free of him; the reply is that the believers also wait, but their waiting is for victory and the triumph of the truth. These authors take the upright path to mean the true religion or the straight road. Al-Mawardi offers two readings: knowledge through victory in this world, or knowledge on the Day of Resurrection of who leads to the Garden. Al-Qurtubi notes that the verse addresses both the waiting unbelievers and the waiting believers who look for victory. On grammar, al-Farra' allowed the word "who" to be in the accusative, but al-Zajjaj and most grammarians reject this and treat it as an interrogative in the nominative. Several readings exist ("al-sawa'", "al-su'a", "al-suway"), which Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan connect to meanings of the middle way, goodness or evil, and which sharpen the contrast between misguidance and guidance. Ibn 'Ashur sees here a hint that the believers are the people of the straight path, and notes that the end of the sura answers its beginning.
